title: The White House and the Market Are Telling Different Stories
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
The political strategist James Carville once joked that if he ended up being reincarnated, he’d like to come back as the bond market. “You can intimidate everybody,” he said

About a month ago, during a talk at Southern Methodist University, the Treasury secretary issued a challenge—both to the business-school students in the audience and to the traders of the world. “I have asymmetric information

I am the house now,” he said. “You can bet against me if you want.” The line was an attempt to explain the government’s decision to boost the Japanese yen over the summer, but it was also a broader statement about his ability to influence markets and guard against financial downturns
This past weekend, Bessent conceded that “the house doesn’t win every hand”—a sign that he’s been slightly chastened

Emphasis on slightly : Although he admitted he “can’t control the bond market,” he maintained that the house still wins “over time.” The bond market’s behavior over the past month clearly called for an adjustment to his posture

The interest rates on the 10-year Treasury (which dictates rates on certain consumer loans) and the 30-year Treasury (an important measure of how investors feel about the government’s ability to pay back its debts) are now the highest they’ve been since 2002
The Trump administration’s market interventions, which have been ramping up in recent months, have had little effect on bond prices
Bessent may continue to insist that he’s the “house,” but it’s clear at this point that the market isn’t listening
The rates on all kinds of everyday loans are closely tied to what goes on in the Treasury market
When holding government debt starts feeling like a riskier proposition, people start demanding bigger payouts—and when yields increase, consumers pay the price
Looking to buy a house? The average rate on a standard 30-year mortgage is now about 7.5 percent, the highest it’s been in almost three years
Mortgage costs are directly tied to the 10-year Treasury note—and before the war in Iran began driving up yields, the average mortgage rate had just dipped under 6 percent
What about a car? CNBC is reporting that rates on auto loans, some of which are already ticking up, are likely to rise even more as yields on five- and 10-year Treasurys continue to spike
Yields are up for a few reasons, one of which has to do with massive ongoing expenditures in the AI sector

Companies are laying the groundwork for decades of further investment in the American tech industry, and the Federal Reserve is expected to respond to the economic boost with higher interest rates to curtail inflation
Inflation is a major concern for traders—it has jolted upward as a result of the Iran war, making the Fed even more hawkish
Yields may also be up because of concerns about the $40 trillion national debt
The deficit is about 6 percent of GDP right now, and the government’s borrowing costs are skyrocketing; it currently spends more on debt financing than it does on defense or Medicare
Although there’s some debate around how much the current deficit panic is affecting bond yields, the market could be signaling that this level of spending is unsustainable
As Bessent rightly points out, he can’t single-handedly determine what happens in the bond market
Over the past couple of months, the Treasury has taken steps to expand its regular bond-buyback program
Usually, these buybacks are intended to keep the Treasury market liquid, but many commentators suspect that these moves were really about managing bond prices
When the government uses its own spending power to purchase Treasurys, it can send a signal to the market that prices ought to go up, and yields ought to come down
Lately, though, the buybacks have had the opposite effect
Despite these supercharged interventions, yields have continued to rise, and Bessent has been taking heat for it on Wall Street
He seems unfazed: “If some of the Bloomberg Terminal bros are unhappy with what I’m doing, well, that’s too bad,” he told Steve Bannon last month
As Bessent digs in, he’s being undercut by his boss’s erratic decision making

Treasury yields tend to go up when foreign bondholders lose trust in the U.S. economy—and Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada, on-again-off-again tariffs, flagrant federal-budget increases, and general air of unpredictability are all points against him. (The president made the unusual suggestion this summer that the military could somehow be used to tame yields.) Plus, the Iran war has driven up consumer prices and raised yields on government debt around the world
Most voters think the president has hurt the economy , and rising borrowing costs won’t make people any happier
In the meantime, the administration doesn’t seem ready to face reality

Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council, said he doesn’t “buy” the negative polling on the economy, and Trump continues to insist that the country is experiencing “the best economy we’ve ever had.” Bessent is doing his part to inspire confidence, but the house seems to be down on its luck
Related: Blame Trump for rising borrowing costs, David Frum argues
Economists who weren’t worried about the debt are now panicking
Here are three new stories from The Atlantic : A Trump rally stuck in time The violence sweeping France was never really about schools
Trump is considering a plan to strike Iran before the midterms

Pike is now conscious and speaking, according to her attorneys, who say she faces a long recovery

title: How Long Until AI Hacks Everything?
excerpt: The Australian government has been scrambling since the revelation that, earlier this year, it was hacked
body: The Australian government has been scrambling since the revelation that, earlier this year, it was hacked

At the United Nations General Assembly last month, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese shared that OpenAI models had, of their own accord, accessed private data from the nation’s Medicare database—in addition to probing or seeking to infiltrate at least three other government agencies

Just this week, Australian lawmakers grilled OpenAI Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon over the incident: “If you hadn’t voluntarily provided that information to government, we still wouldn’t know today?” Senator Jonathon Duniam asked . “What you say is a reasonable conclusion,” Kwon replied

Meanwhile, the country’s government is steeling itself for a future of AI-powered hacks: The Australian Department of Home Affairs has ordered all government agencies to, within the next six months, identify legacy IT systems and establish a plan to phase them out

In a world in which “frontier AI capabilities have targeted the Commonwealth’s technology,” the home-affairs secretary wrote, such software poses “an unacceptable risk to the Australian Government.” Australia is just one of the nations, associations, and private companies bracing for a wave of AI-powered hacks

Criminals and state-sponsored intelligence groups are now using the technology to execute cyberattacks with greater speed, scale, and sophistication—including hyper-personalized phishing emails and automated intrusions

As a result, the number of cybersecurity vulnerabilities disclosed each month has doubled since the start of the year, according to research by Google’s Threat Intelligence Group. [ Read: A startling glimpse at AI’s ruthless efficiency ] In response, IT teams are scrambling to shore up their defenses. “It’s a matter of months, or maybe a year, in which the task of securing the software foundation of civilization will have to be solved,” Stanislav Fort, a former Anthropic researcher who is now the chief scientist at the cybersecurity firm AISLE, told me
And AI is not only making cyberattacks more effective but also increasing the surface area worth hacking
Breaking into a website or executing a ransomware attack takes time, Fort said, so hackers have traditionally chosen large targets with sizable payoffs
But cheap, tireless hacking agents mean any organization or person might be worth targeting

At the same time, the cybersecurity professionals I spoke with were confident they could rise to the occasion. “If we step up our game in cybersecurity, as a field, we can definitely meet the challenge stemming from AI,” Fort said
The cyberattacks on Minnesota water facilities this past summer offer a preview of things to come

Iran-linked hackers disrupted dozens of water utilities in Minnesota, many in small communities that might not have a dedicated cybersecurity person on staff. “We were fortunate that there was a very alert operator that said, ‘Hey, I saw a pump go offline,’” John Israel, Minnesota’s chief information-security officer, told me
The state received a report from the operator around 3 a.m., and within two hours began investigating and responding
The hackers targeted a weakness in industrial computers that had been announced by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency only days earlier

The water utilities temporarily fell back on manual processes to stay operational: For instance, a water operator might have to “drive out to that water tower every few hours” to make sure everything is working, Israel said
Although AI was not directly implicated in the Minnesota cyberattacks, Emily Zimmer, a spokesperson for Minnesota IT Services, told me, “we assume most adversaries use AI” to amplify their attacks
In other words, it’s hard to imagine a hacker not using the technology today

CISA issued an advisory noting threat actors using AI-generated malware to target similar computers in critical infrastructure across the nation. “We’re going to see more vulnerabilities, there’s going to be more patches, and we have to implement them faster in order to prevent those attacks,” Israel said. “And our numbers are showing that that’s the case.” For small towns with small-town budgets defending themselves against nation-state hackers, the challenge is even greater
Minnesota IT Services sends “cybernavigators” around the state to assist with cybersecurity, Israel said, but “hundreds and hundreds of cities and small towns and things” are in need of assistance
An adequate defense from AI attacks demands a paradigm shift in cybersecurity
Historically, IT professionals have had the luxury of time—human defenders just had to move faster than their human adversaries—but AI is enabling far more and far faster attacks

Of course, cybersecurity experts are themselves leveraging AI. “I’m not saying the sky is falling,” Israel said, although he is concerned. “We’ve all got to build capacity on how we respond.” And there is an asymmetry between attackers and defenders
The former use new technologies with abandon, but companies and government agencies tend to be slower and more conservative
Hospitals, for instance, are particularly prized and vulnerable targets for cyberattacks
They store troves of medical records, payment information, and clinical-trial data
Like local water utilities, they can also lack substantial IT resources
Given the risk to patient life from a major outage, clinics are especially likely to pay a ransom

Today, hospitals “have to assume that anything connected to the internet especially is not 100 percent secure,” John Riggi, the national adviser for cybersecurity and risk at the American Hospital Association, told me

Even small facilities have thousands of computers, phones, and medical devices that could be invasion points—so Riggi helps not only secure their IT but also prepare them to operate using analog methods in the event of a debilitating hack
Additionally, hospitals have to be particularly careful in adopting defenses against AI
A clinic cannot implement new code without making sure it won’t disable its ventilators, drug-infusion pumps, X-ray machines, and other crucial devices, Riggi said
Tech companies like to “move fast and break things,” Scott Gee, the AHA’s deputy national adviser for cybersecurity and risk, told me. “In the health-care field, those things are people
We cannot move fast and break them.” Hackers’ odds of coming out ahead are getting better and better
AI is allowing them to both exploit more quickly and automate an actual intrusion
Organizations used to have a month to patch vulnerabilities before they were in serious danger, Adam Meyers, the senior vice president of counter-adversary operations at Crowdstrike, told me
Now they might have only 24 hours to make a fix, he said

And that could “get driven down to the point that you’ve got 30 minutes to patch when a new vulnerability comes out.” A hospital, electrical grid, water system, and really any facility providing important services in real time simply can’t risk implementing new code that quickly

When we spoke, Riggi and Gee were coming off a weekend spent helping hospitals shield themselves against widespread hacks that targeted security flaws in Citrix NetScaler, a platform Riggi told me some 50 percent of hospitals use
NetScaler is “equivalent to air-traffic control” for digital information flowing in a hospital, he said

title: Trump Is Considering a Plan to Strike Iran Before the Midterms
excerpt: Sign up for our newsletter about national security here
body: Sign up for our newsletter about national security here
A fter months of on-again, off-again fighting, the United States hasn’t struck Iran in several weeks

The stretch of relative tranquility is coinciding with the final phase of the midterm-election campaign, and the assumption has been that President Trump will want to keep it going through November 3 so as not to remind voters of an unpopular war that is dragging Republican candidates down nationwide
The White House has asked the Pentagon to develop strike options against Iranian targets that could be exercised ahead of the midterms, according to two administration officials
The planning underscores just how much the president wants to reduce gas prices and demonstrate progress in the conflict before the vote, administration officials told us
The size and targets of the potential strikes—and whether the administration will ultimately proceed—are still being debated
Central Command, which is coordinating the war effort, a U.S. official told us

Even the plans’ advocates acknowledge that limited strikes would not, by themselves, bring Iran to the negotiating table, restore safe travel through the Strait of Hormuz, or lower gas prices before Election Day

But those in favor believe that further action after months of uneasy peace could allow Trump to demonstrate strength and potentially declare some sort of victory, giving Republicans much-needed momentum heading into the election. “It would make the president look like he got a win and that gas prices would start going down,” a Republican familiar with the deliberations told us after being granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters
A limited operation could be followed up by more substantial military action after the midterms, when Trump has suggested that the conflict, which is now in its eighth month, could resume
Any strike campaign would put the roughly 50,000 U.S. troops in the region, as well as Gulf allies, at risk of Iranian retaliation, and further deplete America’s munitions stockpiles
Even some of the president’s most ardent supporters want the U.S. to exit the war in order to halt the rise in inflation
An inconclusive limited strike is likely to have the opposite effect
Crude-oil prices have typically risen when the U.S. has resumed strikes after a pause, according to the U.S

Energy Information Administration . “Military action has done nothing to drive down oil prices; in fact, it has done the opposite,” Will Walldorf, an international-affairs professor at Wake Forest University and a senior fellow at the think tank Defense Priorities, told us. “And if this is an attempt to rally the Republican vote, how does that make any sense given how unpopular this war is?” T he president has repeatedly discussed the possibility of resuming strikes after the election, threatening in a speech to the United Nations last month to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” if Iran did not reach a deal

In an interview with Time magazine released earlier this month, the president reiterated that post-election strikes were possible, saying “we’ve been stocking up for the last six months.” Last week, Trump said he believed the U.S. would win the war “right after the election,” though he added, “Maybe before the election.” Republican candidates see the conflict, and the high gas prices it has caused, as a severe drag on their prospects for keeping a majority in the House and Senate

Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate from Texas, has privately complained that the war has hurt his campaign, telling donors last month that rising gas and diesel prices caused by the conflict were “by far our biggest problem,” according to Axios . [ Read: The real reason Trump wants economic sanctions in Iran ] In recent weeks, the Pentagon has presented Trump with a series of options that would restart hostilities after the midterms, and now Centcom is compiling options for pre-midterm strikes
The post-election menu ranges from small strikes to massive attacks, including further blows to Iran’s energy industry

Even though the Trump administration remains bullish on the effectiveness of its economic pressure campaign, officials caution that Iran may wait several more months before entering serious negotiations
Trump has been publicly furious about the war’s persistence and is believed by those close to him to feel privately humiliated by his inability to bring the conflict to a successful conclusion
He has signaled to aides that he would be willing to strike Iran again, though his advisers believe that the right moment would be after the midterms rather than before
The war is deeply unpopular, and Republicans would not welcome the conflict’s return to the headlines, according to GOP strategists, particularly if more American lives are lost

A White House official stressed to us that Trump “has all options available at any time,” adding that “things will go one of two ways; the easy way or the hard way.” The official did not address our questions about the timing of possible strikes
Oil prices surged after the Iran war began, climbing as high as nearly $118 a barrel in the spring
And although they briefly topped $100 a barrel last month, they have been hovering around $100 a barrel

Gas prices dipped slightly earlier this week amid reports of more tanker traffic transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway that carried one-fifth of the world’s oil supply before Iran closed it early in the war

The White House and Republicans facing reelection harbor the hope that further incremental drops will signal lower prices ahead, giving the party some relief before the vote. [ Read: Trump is preparing for a long war ] But Iran has been persistent in its attacks
Earlier this week, it targeted a series of ships attempting to transit the strait, prompting some shipowners to reconsider use of the route
White House officials view those recent attacks as a deliberate swipe at the president, according to people familiar with the West Wing’s thinking
The administration has also said it would release oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in an effort to increase supplies and keep gasoline prices from rising further
Americans are now paying an average of $4.37 a gallon for gas, according to AAA, compared with just below $3 before the U.S. and Israeli strike campaign began February 28
T he latest military deliberations come as the administration pursues two tracks at once: ongoing military and economic pressure, and indirect negotiations

Washington and Tehran continue to communicate through mediators, but significant differences remain over the terms and sequencing of a cease-fire, an end to the U.S. blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the strait’s reopening
Iran may already be anticipating renewed U.S. strikes
Earlier this week, the U.S. removed B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Britain because U.S. intelligence indicated a possible Iranian-linked attack on the base

Iran has denied any involvement. “Iran is watching the calendar and knows the election is coming,” said one adviser who spoke with us. “And they want to stick it to the president.” At the same time, the White House believes that Tehran is at its weakest point since the conflict began, two administration officials told us
One close Trump adviser told us that the pattern has been that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps appears to be in charge one day, and then somewhat more moderate political officials the next
Overall, the hard-liners seem to have the upper hand, the officials told us, and they have shown little openness to a deal or even to softening their position
Yet some in Trump’s orbit believe that the moment is rapidly approaching when even the hard-liners may be forced to concede

A strike before the midterms could be seen as a not-so-gentle nudge in that direction—but it could also achieve the opposite, and put the war and its consequences front and center just as Americans cast their votes.

title: Why American Cities Cost So Much and Deliver So Little
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his thoughts on the sudden rec
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his thoughts on the sudden recall of 12 B-1 bombers from their base in the south of England to the mainland of the United States
He asks what prompted the move and why the Trump administration refuses to learn vital military lessons from Ukraine
Then, David is joined by Reihan Salam, the president of the Manhattan Institute for Policy Research, to discuss why American cities cost so much and often deliver so little
They explore how some urban governments waste public money, how cities could provide better services to residents, and why the rise of populism is doing little to solve Americans’ actual problems
Finally, David ends the episode with a discussion of Every War Must End by Fred Charles Iklé

The following is a transcript of the episode: Reihan Salam: Well, David, I actually don’t believe that it is Donald Trump who is the only political figure who will have been discredited by this moment
When you’re looking at the Democratic coalition right now, I see a lot of anger and frustration with how people see their leadership class as well
So I think that this is going to be this big generational turnover that could go very badly. [ Music ] David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show
I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic

My guest this week will be Reihan Salam, president of the Manhattan Institute, and we’ll discuss how American cities can deliver better government to their residents at more reasonable costs than they now do
This week’s book will be a masterpiece of strategic thinking: Every War Must End by Fred Charles Iklé

But before either the dialogue or the book discussion, some opening thoughts on a news story you may have seen this past weekend: the sudden recall of 12 B-1 bombers from their base in the south of England to the mainland of the United States
As so often with Trump-administration military stories, there may be less, or there may be more, to this story than meets the eye
The Trump administration is staffed by people who look for any opportunity and any excuse to recall military assets from allies, and especially from European allies, back to the American mainland
This recall may be something that people in the Trump administration wanted to do anyway, for their own reason
And we’ll find out more about that in the days ahead
But the first reports may also be true—that there was some sudden threat to these bombers that necessitated their removal from England back to the American mainland
What might that threat be? Either a terrorist attack in Britain, or else possibly a drone-and-missile attack like those that have been experienced by American forces in the Persian Gulf
But what we do know is that through the Persian Gulf, the Iranians have had great success, much greater success than as first reported, pushing back American forces from their perimeters
The American naval base in Bahrain was badly damaged by Iranian drones and missiles

As we have seen in Ukraine, suddenly individuals far from the battle scene controlling these small, comparatively inexpensive new technologies can inflict tremendous damage anywhere on the enemy’s territory
The Ukrainians have done it to Russia, and the Russians have done it to the Ukrainians
We may be living through a revolution in military technology as dramatic as when the advent of gunpowder made obsolete the knight on horseback and the castle made of stone
The United States is poorly adapted to this revolution, and especially poorly adapted under the Trump administration
There are deep reasons why the United States is poorly adapted to this revolution
The United States has made an enormous investment in very costly, very sophisticated platforms: bombers, fighters, aircraft carriers, tanks, equipment
Machinery that moves aboveground, on the land, on the ocean, in the air
And it is reluctant to accept that this enormous investment may now be obsolete, and obsolete in ways that empower weaker adversaries who master the new technology of drone warfare first
The United States is also poorly adapted because of the way America finances and approves its military technology

The congressional system—the iron triangle of lobbyists and administrations and Congress—tends to regard weapons as not just tools of war, but also as tools of economic development back at home, and oftentimes as income-support strategies for retired members of the military
And so the United States invests very deeply in systems that are driven by domestic needs and not by the needs of the battlefield
In the Trump era, these difficulties are augmented by two special problems
The first is the nation that is the pioneer and leader in drone warfare is Ukraine
And the United States under President Trump is terribly reluctant, brutally reluctant, to learn lessons of war from Ukraine

President Trump, Vice President Vance, and others around them decided early that the Ukrainians were losers, that they were doomed, that they were dependents, they were welfare recipients, they were moochers, they deserved nothing, and they had nothing to offer

Now it turns out they may be the leading military innovator of the modern era, and suddenly it’s very embarrassing to turn around and say, maybe these guys, of whom the Trump administration has so little good to say, maybe they have something to offer that America needs
So the reluctance to learn lessons from Ukraine—and the eagerness to fire the generals and admirals most ready to learn the lessons from Ukraine—that has handicapped the United States
There’s another handicap in the drone-warfare era, and that is ideological
Secretary Hegseth is a man with a vision of the military as a tool for waging culture war, not real battlefield warfare
He has inveighed against troops who wear beards, against troops who are overweight, against troops who don’t have enough testosterone

Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds

Drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their GLP-1 drugs age less quickly, according to molecular “aging clocks” that track changes in DNA or levels of key proteins.  The findings add to speculation that GLP-1 drugs could be acting on basic causes of aging and might be true longevity treatments

But how much can we read into these results? Read the full story on what the new findings reveal about GLP-1 drugs and aging . —Antonio Regalado 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Energy Dome and its carbon dioxide batteries Energy Dome is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers
Solar and wind are among the cheapest and quickest ways to add electricity to the grid
But they’re subject to variations in weather patterns, so supplies can be intermittent
Energy Dome has an unusual solution: massive batteries that use compressed carbon dioxide to store energy for when the grid needs it
Compressing gas to store energy isn’t new
Utilities have used compressed air in underground caverns to hang on to reserves for decades
But Energy Dome’s approach doesn’t require any specific geology to work, so it could be more easily scaled to help grids around the world

Here’s how the company is using carbon dioxide to store renewable energy . —Casey Crownhart Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from mobile flood barriers and electric buses to next-generation nuclear reactors

MIT Technology Review Narrated: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason —Thore Graepel, a core member of DeepMind’s AlphaGo team Ten years ago, I watched a program I helped build stun the world by beating Go champion Lee Sedol
AlphaGo won after making a move so strange that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch
It was AlphaGo’s powers of reasoning that made this creative choice—and these are powers that today’s AI lacks.  This is why I recently left my position at Google DeepMind
I believe we need a fresh approach to machine reasoning, one that draws on AlphaGo’s architecture
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts
Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released

title: Many drugs have mirror chemical structures, one helpful and the other harmful – a Nobel-winning discovery allows chemists to make either on demand
url:
<title>Many drugs have mirror chemical structures, one helpful and the other harmful – a Nobel-winning discovery allows chemists to make either on demand</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764706/original/file-20261007-50-rki63q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=163%2C0%2C2972%2C1981&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Some molecules have &#39;mirror images,&#39; and while one form can be helpful, the other can be harmful. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/nonribosomal-amino-acid-synthesis-only-the-amino-acid-on-news-photo/151050617?phrase=chiral%20molecules&amp;adppopup=true">BSIP/UIG Via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The effects a drug or chemical compound have on the body depend on how its atoms are arranged in space. Some compounds have a dark twin with the same molecular formula but different 3D structure – and this can have consequences for what they do or don’t do in the body.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2026/press-release/">2026 Nobel Prize in chemistry</a> was awarded to two researchers who developed a chemical process allowing them to create only one of these two twins. Called <a href="https://books.rsc.org/books/edited-volume/1992/Asymmetric-AutocatalysisThe-Soai-Reaction">asymmetric organic synthesis</a>, this discovery meant that chemists developing pharmaceuticals could create one version or the other – for example, only the version of the molecule that benefits the body, not the version that can cause damage.</p>

<p>Consider the tragic story of <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2013/09/23/booming/the-death-and-afterlife-of-thalidomide.html">thalidomide</a>, a morning sickness drug that caused thousands of birth defects and miscarriages. While <a href="https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/molecule-of-the-week/archive/t/thalidomide.html">one form</a>, or isomer, of thalidomide has a sedative effect, the other is thought to cause abnormal physiological development. Because the two versions can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1417832112">convert back and forth in the body</a>, it’s dangerous to take either form of thalidomide while pregnant.</p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=dChGtb0AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">My research</a> has focused on one such compound found in red grapes and peanuts: resveratrol. It has been a scientific mystery why clinical trials on using resveratrol to treat Alzheimer’s disease have had inconsistent results. With the help of the chemical reactions that led to the 2026 Nobel Prize, my team and I discovered that it may be because <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-30785-8">two different forms were used</a> – while one may help with cognition and memory, the other may be toxic to the nervous system. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/41n3mDoVbvk?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Thalidomide has since been repurposed to treat other conditions, including cancer.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Isomers and amino acids</h2>

<p>Many drugs have the same atoms and bonds but are arranged differently in space. These drugs are called <a href="https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/chemical-processes/stereochemistry/a/chiral-drugs">chiral</a> compounds – meaning they exist as two nonsuperimposable mirror images. For example, your hands are also nonsuperimposable mirror images of each other. Although they look the same, they don’t overlap when you put one on top of the other. </p>

<p>Usually these mirror-image versions have very similar properties because they share the same elements and bonds. But the way they are arranged in space can drastically change the effects they have in the body. Just as you wouldn’t be able to fit a left-handed glove on your right hand, a left-handed version of a drug wouldn’t be able to fit into a target in the body shaped to fit a right-handed molecule.</p>

<p>Chiral molecules come in two versions, or isomers, defined by their <a href="https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/chemical-processes/stereochemistry/a/chiral-drugs">optical activity</a>. This means that if you shine polarized light on a chiral molecule, one will rotate the light to the left (indicated by the prefix L-, or levorotatory) while the other will rotate it to the right (indicated by the prefix D, or dextrorotatory).</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nature.com/scitable/topicpage/an-evolutionary-perspective-on-amino-acids-14568445/">Amino acids</a>, the building blocks of proteins, are chiral molecules. Living organisms primarily make proteins from <a href="https://atlasofscience.org/l-amino-acids-key-for-the-evolution-of-life-came-from-extraterrestrial-space/">amino acids with L configurations</a>. The D configuration, however, has many other functions in nature. <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fmicb.2018.00683">Bacteria</a>, for example, use D configuration amino acids to make their cell walls. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00726-020-02892-7">Mammals</a> use D configuration amino acids as messengers in their nervous and endocrine systems.  </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Bw_cetheReo?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The structure of a compound matters just as much as its individual atoms and bonds.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The amino acid tyrosine is one important exception to the L configuration rule. Unlike other amino acids, both the L and D configurations of tyrosine can be activated for protein synthesis by an enzyme called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-2836(67)90259-8">tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase (TyrRS)</a>. </p>

<p>The presence of D-tyrosine can make it difficult for cells to synthesize proteins that only use L-tyrosine. However, cells have evolved enzymes that can discriminate between both versions and ensure that only L-tyrosine is used. When tyrosine-consuming enzymes are absent, the resulting increased levels of tyrosine in the body can have <a href="https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/tyrosinemia/">toxic effects</a>, including <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199002153220704">damage to the nervous system</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-30785-8">Recently published work</a> from my lab suggests a potential reason why too much tyrosine can be neurotoxic. When we added increasing amounts of L-tyrosine to rat brain cells in a petri dish, we found that it decreased levels of TyrRS, the enzyme that activates tyrosine to make proteins without causing damage to the body. Surprisingly, adding D-tyrosine not only caused TyrRS levels to drop, but also killed the neurons.</p>

<p>When we looked at the brains of Alzheimer’s patients who show increased tyrosine levels, we also found that TyrRS enzyme levels are depleted. Our hypothesis is that as tyrosine levels in the brain increase, TyrRS enzyme levels drop and cause damaging effects on the brains of those with Alzheimer’s. These findings indicate the potentially important role TyrRS may play in the synthesis of proteins essential for cognition and memory.</p>

<h2>Grapes, peanuts and Alzheimer’s</h2>

<p>These findings have implications for studies on <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390%2Fbiomedicines6030091">resveratrol</a>, a compound found in red wine that researchers have been examining for potential health benefits. While <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trci.2018.09.009">some clinical trials</a> found that resveratrol can improve cognitive function in people with Alzheimer’s disease, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000002035">others found it had the opposite effect</a> and made the disease more severe. Why resveratrol can have such varying effects has remained a scientific enigma.</p>

<p>Resveratrol comes in two forms, cis-resveratrol and trans-resveratrol. The <a href="https://courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-mcc-organicchemistry/chapter/geometric-stereoisomers-cistrans/">“cis-” and “trans-” prefixes</a>, much like L- and D-, describe how the same atoms in two isomers are arranged differently in space. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">At low concentrations, the trans form of resveratrol, left, can switch to the cis form, right.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rasveratrol_isomerization.png">V8rik/Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>My colleagues and I found that because the two forms of resveratrol <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11357-020-00295-w">bind to TyrRS in different ways</a>, they can result in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-30785-8">opposite effects in neurons</a>. While cis-resveratrol was able to increase TyrRS levels in rat neurons in a petri dish, high concentrations of trans-resveratrol depleted TyrRS and caused neural damage. However, low concentrations of trans-resveratrol can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14028">convert into cis-resveratrol</a> in the body. This result leads to an increase in TyrRS levels and its associated benefits.</p>

<p>We hypothesize that many clinical trials on resveratrol failed because none tested cis-resveratrol alone. We believe that this may also explain why trials that used high doses of trans-resveratrol saw harmful effects, while trials that used low doses of trans-resveratrol that were then converted into cis-resveratrol in the body saw beneficial effects.</p>

<p>Beyond the individual atoms and bonds of molecules, the body also cares about how they’re arranged in space. Paying attention to the different forms a drug takes could help lead to more effective treatments.</p>

title: From jargon to impact: Teaching undergraduates the art of public communication
url:
<title>From jargon to impact: Teaching undergraduates the art of public communication</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764305/original/file-20261006-50-q03d08.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Undergraduates can learn the benefits of applying research to broader societal questions through public writing.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/search/2/image-film?agreements=pa%3A220881&amp;family=creative&amp;phrase=University%20students%20writing%20and%20learning&amp;sort=best&amp;excludenudity=true&amp;suppressfamilycorrection=true">FatCamera via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Articles published in The Conversation go well beyond academics writing for a general audience – they can also serve as great content for educators to use in the classroom.</p>

<p>Our recent article in the academic journal <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/00330124.2026.2627445">The Professional Geographer</a> explores how articles from The Conversation provide opportunities for public storytelling and authentic learning in university classrooms.</p>

<p>As geographers and experienced writers for The Conversation – having written or co-written 26 articles since 2017 – we understand firsthand the value of disseminating these short, open-access articles that can be <a href="https://theconversation.com/us/republishing-guidelines">easily republished under the Creative Commons license</a>.</p>

<p>To this point, one of the top republishers for The Conversation is <a href="https://www.mheducation.com/prek-12/program/microsites/actively-learn.html">Actively Learn</a>, a McGraw Hill platform used to provide standards-aligned content for K–12 educators.</p>

<p>Yet we feel that The Conversation’s potential contributions to university education have not been sufficiently explored, which is unexpected given that its articles are authored by college teachers and researchers.</p>

<h2>Why it matters</h2>

<p>Public storytelling is increasingly important for scholars as higher education faces <a href="https://www.aaup.org/issues-higher-education/political-attacks-higher-education">increased scrutiny</a>, <a href="https://www.highereddive.com/news/us-higher-ed-faces-mounting-attacks-on-academic-freedom-report-warns/830730/">politicized attacks on truth-telling</a>, <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeltnietzel/2026/10/02/percentage-of-americans-seeing-college-as-very-important-hits-record-low/">pressure to show broader relevance</a> and <a href="https://www.insidehighered.com/news/institutions/2026/06/16/colleges-must-act-now-regain-public-trust-aacu-says">calls to regain trust</a>.</p>

<p>In our article, we argue for integrating more public-facing science communication into educational spaces. We also introduce our use of articles from The Conversation as a classroom tool and discuss coaching students through challenges they face.</p>

<p>Our pedagogical work may interest university educators in other fields looking for ways to engage their classrooms in “<a href="https://ablconnect.harvard.edu/authentic-learning">authentic learning</a>” – that is, learning in real-world contexts – and incorporate public storytelling into the professional preparation of their students.</p>

<p>Authentic learning gives students opportunities to observe how subject experts apply academic research to address social, political and environmental issues and contribute to public and policy debates and decisions beyond the classroom.</p>

<p>We choose to use articles from The Conversation in pedagogical exercises because we want to challenge students to confront societal issues from new perspectives. The goal is to do our part as university educators to help produce scholar-citizens ready for civic engagement.</p>

<h2>Opportunity for a final deliverable</h2>

<p>For example, in an end-of-semester writing assignment we have hosted, students were tasked with selecting a pressing issue in the course’s scope and writing a short article in the style of The Conversation.</p>

<p>Students were asked to draft a “pitch” for an article before writing it, just like prospective authors do for The Conversation. They were asked to make revisions, think through how to support their claims with evidence and adapt to the various conventions of writing for the public, similar to how it may go in working with the editorial team.</p>

<p>Although it is a sometimes difficult and often humbling process for the students to go through, they in real time understand the struggle of writing concisely and interestingly for a general audience.</p>

<p>They also produce a well-written short article that they can be proud of and potentially publish in an appropriate outlet or include in a portfolio for a potential employer.</p>

<p>Although The Conversation does not allow undergraduate students or community partners to go through the process of submitting a pitch and drafting an article to be published, our previous students have shown their ability to punch above their weight and produce short articles that demonstrate their applied and rigorous understanding of course concepts.</p>

<h2>Why we write</h2>

<p>As scholars, we like to write for The Conversation for four primary reasons:</p>

<p>First, we love the challenge of taking our discipline-specific academic work and translating it into jargon-free, accessible writing that anyone in our family or community could easily read.</p>

<p>This can be a difficult process – especially in taking complex academic concepts and breaking them down into simpler language while keeping essential rigor and nuance. The editors we work with from The Conversation are helpful in this case – even if the process is sometimes maddening along the way.</p>

<p>Second, we love tracking the readership of the published pieces in The Conversation’s dashboard portal. It is exciting to see a recently published article cross a threshold, such as 70,000 reads, over a period of time – something you would never experience from a traditionally published academic journal article.</p>

<p>These aren’t just numbers for us – it’s an indication of the potential impact of our work.</p>

<p>Third, we love how easy it is to share our articles via social media or via DOI links. Additionally, when other news and media outlets republish our pieces via the Creative Commons license, our work gets disseminated widely.</p>

<p>There is no paywall preventing access, no login or account required. Our wider communities can read the short piece by simply clicking a link that can be texted to them.</p>

<p>Fourth, our previous articles published in The Conversation are great sources for assigned reading in our seminar courses. They often cover content that we teach in our courses and are written in our voices. They also are short and easy to read for busy students – while laden with helpful hyperlinks to sources to explore further.</p>

<p>Writing for The Conversation allows us to produce accessible course content that we can use and share for years to come. From our experiences, students who read the articles have enjoyed them as much as we do, because they are quick reads and written in an interesting and accessible manner.</p>

<h2>What is next</h2>

<p>Further research studies could be done to quantitatively measure student learning outcomes when using articles from The Conversation.</p>

<p>Although <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/00330124.2026.2627445">our published article</a> is helpful in providing anecdotal insights of the results we have seen from our experiences, more research would allow for further ways to measure the impact of using these articles in the classroom.</p>

<p>We believe The Conversation can help higher education even further by having teams or boards of educators working together to assemble college classroom e-books of articles organized around certain themes of instruction. This expansion of academic insights can help our students, who represent future civic decision-makers and public storytellers.</p>

<p>Regardless of future research opportunities, educators can choose to integrate articles from The Conversation into their classrooms now – whether using these articles for assigned content reading or for creative writing exercises.</p>

<p>We have seen firsthand the benefits of doing so, and we encourage more educators to join us. In doing so, your students can join the broader public conversation – with the power of The Conversation.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293752/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
</content>

<title>These state supreme court races could decide abortion access and trans rights</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763944/original/file-20261005-50-mceur1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C3%2C6015%2C4010&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Whoever wins state judicial races in November will not just be interpreting the law. They will be writing the next chapter of it.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/voting-booths-with-no-people-royalty-free-image/2013953851?phrase=Vote%20US%20elections&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Stefania Pelfini la Waziya/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In the heated news coverage of what’s at stake in <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/2026-midterms-184240">the 2026 midterms</a>, state supreme court races are drawing relatively little attention. Yet these are highly significant elections.</p>

<p>Thirty-one states are holding supreme court elections in 2026, with voters nationwide picking judges to fill more than 60 open seats.</p>

<p>As a law professor whose <a href="https://law.utexas.edu/faculty/rachel-rebouche/">research and writing focuses on reproductive health</a>, I’m watching these races closely. That’s because in the coming years these courts will have the final word on many consequential legal fights around abortion and trans healthcare.</p>

<h2>State supreme court judges make high-stakes decisions</h2>

<p>When the <a href="https://rewirenewsgroup.com/2022/06/24/the-day-roe-died/">U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022</a>, ending a half-century of federal constitutional protection for abortion, it handed this major issue back to the states. As a result, in addition to prompting ballot initiatives, the court’s decision in <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/2021/19-1392">Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization</a> has also spurred litigation in state courts.</p>

<p>These cases ask judges to discern, for example, whether state constitutions <a href="https://rewirenewsgroup.com/2026/09/14/indiana-supreme-court-hears-religious-freedom-challenge-to-state-abortion-law/">create a right to abortion</a> – or, at least, <a href="https://www.arkansasonline.com/news/2026/sep/28/judge-hears-arguments-in-lawsuit-challenging/">prohibit restrictions on abortion access</a>.</p>

<p>Moreover, in weighing the <a href="https://19thnews.org/2026/09/texas-abortion-lawsuit-ken-paxton-tierra-walker/">legality of abortion bans</a>, state judges must determine specific issues of abortion access. <a href="https://www.newsfromthestates.com/article/idaho-supreme-court-approves-state-officials-re-drafted-abortion-ballot-initiative-language">Idaho’s high court recently approved</a> Republican officials’ rewritten wording for a ballot initiative that would repeal the state’s abortion ban; advocates for the initiative argue that the language misrepresents Idaho’s abortion law.</p>

<p>In Indiana, <a href="https://www.newsfromthestates.com/article/indiana-supreme-court-weighs-limits-religious-exemptions-abortion-ban">the state Supreme Court recently heard arguments</a> over whether a religious freedom law creates an exception to the state’s near-total abortion ban. The plaintiffs in that case argued that their faiths allowed or required the procedure in circumstances the ban currently forbids.</p>

<p>Increasingly, the U.S. Supreme Court has been handing questions concerning transgender rights back to states, too.</p>

<p>In June 2025, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/24pdf/23-477_2cp3.pdf">United States v. Skrmetti</a> that Tennessee’s ban on puberty blockers and hormone therapy for transgender minors does not count as sex discrimination under the U.S. Constitution. Consequently, that and similar bans only need to pass the lowest level of judicial review; they no longer have to pass the higher bar of “strict scrutiny.”</p>

<p>This means lower courts can essentially rubber-stamp the bans that state legislatures have passed. In fact, the <a href="https://rewirenewsgroup.com/2025/06/24/how-the-supreme-court-blessed-anti-trans-discrimination/">Skrmetti decision cleared the way</a> for the roughly two dozen states with similar bans to keep enforcing them.</p>

<p>Skrmetti did not, however, require any state to pass such a law. And it does not address how far the ruling extends to adults or whether it applies to other related aspects of gender-affirming care, such as insurance coverage.</p>

<p>In other words, the people who now decide whether abortion restrictions stay on the books or whether a minor can get gender-affirming care are, in many cases, not justices sitting on the U.S. Supreme Court. In many cases, they will be state supreme court judges.</p>

            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763947/original/file-20261005-50-sl3gpc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An illustration depicts an American flag, a voter casting a ballot and the scales of justice." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763947/original/file-20261005-50-sl3gpc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763947/original/file-20261005-50-sl3gpc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=317&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763947/original/file-20261005-50-sl3gpc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=317&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763947/original/file-20261005-50-sl3gpc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=317&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763947/original/file-20261005-50-sl3gpc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763947/original/file-20261005-50-sl3gpc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763947/original/file-20261005-50-sl3gpc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/election-law-royalty-free-image/1911373147?phrase=Judicial%20races%20US%20elections&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">wildpixel/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>North Carolina, Georgia, Michigan, Montana have races to watch</h2>

<p>In Montana, judicial races could change the ideological bent of the state’s top court. Judicial elections in the state are technically nonpartisan, but Republicans see a chance to retake the state Supreme Court with judges they endorse.</p>

<p>In 2023, its Democrat-endorsed majority <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/montana/supreme-court/2023/da-22-0207-0.html">ruled that the state constitution protects abortion</a> rights. It also determined that attempts to stop one class of health providers – advanced practice registered nurses – from performing abortions violated those rights.</p>

<p>Judges who upheld restrictions affecting residents’ reproductive rights will face voters this fall in <a href="https://boltsmag.org/your-state-by-state-guide-to-the-2026-supreme-court-elections/">Alabama, Arizona, Florida, North Dakota, Oklahoma and Texas</a>. In some of these races, abortion is a live – and legally dynamic – issue.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nccourts.gov/courts/supreme-court">North Carolina’s high court</a> also leans heavily conservative. This year one of just two Democrats on the seven-judge panel – incumbent Democrat Anita Earls – is up for reelection. If she loses, the GOP would gain a near-total supermajority on North Carolina’s Supreme Court. That outcome would likely cement the party’s edge on key political matters for years to come.</p>

<p>Michigan looks like the mirror image of North Carolina. All justices there are officially nonpartisan, but <a href="https://www.michiganpublic.org/politics-government/2026-08-06/have-questions-about-judicial-elections-this-will-help">Democrat-backed justices hold a 6-1 majority</a> on the seven-member court. Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh and Justice Noah Hood – both Democrats – are up for reelection this fall.</p>

<p>Democrats are hoping to retain their edge, in part to keep abortion protected. Voters <a href="https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-Article-I-28">enshrined abortion rights directly into Michigan’s Constitution</a> in 2022, and the state’s highest court has already interpreted that amendment to dismiss <a href="https://www.wkar.org/wkar-news/2023-05-11/michigan-supreme-court-dismisses-last-of-abortion-related-cases">abortion-related restrictions</a>.</p>

<h2>Ohio protects abortion, but courts will decide how much</h2>

<p>Ohio is a powerful example of what is at stake in this year’s state supreme court races. Republicans hold a 6-1 majority on the state’s high court, a dominant position built over successive election cycles in 2022 and 2024.</p>

<p>In the 2026 midterms, Ohio’s only Democratic state Supreme Court justice, Jennifer Brunner, is <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Ohio_Supreme_Court_elections,_2026">defending her seat against a Republican challenger</a>. If Brunner loses, Ohio’s highest court could become a unanimous conservative bench – one that will likely determine the outcome of high-profile cases related to both abortion access and gender-affirming care.</p>

<p>Ohio voters <a href="https://apnews.com/article/ohio-abortion-amendment-election-2023-fe3e06747b616507d8ca21ea26485270">approved a constitutional amendment in 2023 protecting abortion access</a>. The amendment establishes that individuals have the right to make their own reproductive decisions. The language covers contraception, fertility treatment, continuing a pregnancy, miscarriage care and abortion up to fetal viability. It also asserts that the state generally cannot interfere with these decisions.</p>

<p>Now, lower courts are <a href="https://www.statenews.org/government-politics/2026-08-20/both-sides-of-abortion-debate-say-latest-ohio-supreme-court-action-on-amendment-wont-be-the-last">litigating whether restrictions on abortion access</a> – for instance, the state’s 24-hour waiting period and ban on telehealth for medication abortion – can survive scrutiny under that amendment.</p>

<p>The Ohio Supreme Court may eventually decide that case. In my assessment, an even more conservative Ohio court might be inclined to read the voter-approved abortion amendment as narrowly as possible. </p>

<p>Ohio’s Supreme Court is similarly poised to make big decisions on trans rights. For example, it could uphold the state’s ban on gender-affirming care for transgender minors. That would reverse <a href="https://statecourtreport.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/ohio-court-strikes-down-ban-gender-affirming-care-minors">a 2025 appellate ruling</a> that had struck down the law, which was passed over the veto of Republican Gov. Mike DeWine.</p>

<p>Even if they don’t change the partisan makeup of these courts, elections for state supreme court seats in places such as Ohio may matter for the scope and breadth of rulings that claw back individual rights. Or they may foretell how a conservative near-supermajority might lock in abortion and trans restrictions for a generation.</p>

<p>Whoever wins these judicial races in November will not just be interpreting the law. In a real sense, they will be writing the next chapter of it.</p>

<title>Why your boss matters more than remote or hybrid work when it comes to burnout and job satisfaction</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764243/original/file-20261006-50-k340tr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1099%2C3768%2C2512&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Long-standing factors contributing to job satisfaction, such as feeling appreciated, still matter more than the type of workplace format.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/man-covered-in-sticky-notes-at-office-desk-mlVbMbxfWI4">Luis Villasmil on Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The post-pandemic push to bring workers back to the office has left many nostalgic for more <a href="https://theconversation.com/hybrid-work-is-not-always-the-golden-compromise-employees-expect-even-as-more-companies-implement-it-283015">flexible arrangements</a>, such as hybrid or remote work. </p>

<p>But a wealth of data since the pandemic now suggests that <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-employers-can-make-good-decisions-about-remote-work-before-the-next-crisis-strikes-282671">workplace factors</a> like feeling appreciated and having a good relationship with your manager are much more tied to job satisfaction than the actual time spent in the office. </p>

<p>To understand this insight, it’s important to recognize that a return to the office can mean very different things to different workers. Someone who values uninterrupted time at home may resent the commute. A younger trainee struggling to learn the job may welcome easier access to colleagues. An employee who dislikes their manager may lament having to see them in person.</p>

<p>These differences help explain why the return-to-office debate often produces conflicting answers. </p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=KKQXJ_8AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">As a researcher</a> of the ways technology is changing the workplace, I co-authored a study with business and accounting scholar <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=D1lDcKYAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Jason Schloetzer</a> that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07017">analyzed responses</a> from nearly 165,000 U.S. employees between 2020 and 2023 from the database Payscale. These surveys let us look beyond location to ask whether employees felt appreciated; considered pay fair and transparent; received useful communication; had chances to develop; and enjoyed a good relationship with their manager. </p>

<p>Once we accounted for these and other job-specific variables, we found that
the edge in satisfaction for fully or mostly remote workers disappears. The only group of employees who felt more satisfied on the job were those who sometimes worked remotely – and that difference was modest. </p>

<p>In other words, long-standing factors shaping job satisfaction outweighed workplace format when it came to making employees happy.</p>

<h2>The workplace behind the work arrangement</h2>

<p>Semi- or fully remote workers <a href="https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/remote-work-happiness-evidence-153351d8">may appear more satisfied</a>. But other factors, such as having better pay or more supportive workplace practices, need to be taken into account, we argue.</p>

<p>Employees’ relationships with their managers is one of those variables. We asked employees to rate the statement “I have a great relationship with my direct manager” on a 5-point scale, with 4 or 5 indicating favorable. The measure reflects the employee’s own assessment rather than a checklist of managerial skills; questions about communication, appreciation and development opportunities were asked separately.</p>

<p>A favorable manager relationship was tied to higher job satisfaction across work arrangements, we found. But that association was stronger among employees working on-site than among those who always or sometimes worked remotely. One possible explanation is that working together gives employees more opportunities to benefit from a supportive manager who mentors and offers development opportunities, while distance can offer some relief when the relationship is less favorable.</p>

<p>We also used data from the Gallup Workplace Panel to study the same workers over time. These results reinforced our findings: It’s important to consider the workplace as a whole when evaluating remote or hybrid work.</p>

<h2>Burnout and happiness are different questions</h2>

<p>Feeling satisfied with a job, however, doesn’t necessarily mean feeling well overall. Someone can like their job while feeling exhausted, or they may appreciate working at home while feeling socially disconnected. That’s why we treat job satisfaction, burnout and happiness as separate values, and why we distinguish stress on a particular day from persistent work exhaustion.</p>

<p>Looking at stress, for example, we found that it’s common across work arrangements. According to <a href="https://www.gallup.com/workplace/697904/state-of-the-global-workplace-global-data.aspx">Gallup’s 2026 State of the Global Workplace report</a>, 41% of fully remote employees reported substantial stress the previous day, compared with 46% of hybrid employees, as well as 46% of on-site employees whose jobs could be done remotely. </p>

<p>Feeling satisfied with a job, however, doesn’t necessarily mean feeling well overall. Someone can value their work while finding its demands exhausting. Job satisfaction, daily stress and burnout capture different aspects of that experience.</p>

<p>Physicians are one example. Among physicians whose organizations participated in an <a href="https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/physician-health/us-physician-burnout-hits-lowest-rate-covid-19">American Medical Association survey</a> in 2024, about three-quarters reporting being satisfied with their job, while almost half reported feeling a great deal of stress because of their job, such as from burdensome paperwork or staff shortages. </p>

<p>The published summary doesn’t identify exactly how many doctors reported both, but it shows that satisfaction and widespread stress can coexist within a profession. </p>

<p>Meanwhile, separate <a href="https://www.gallup.com/workplace/237059/employee-burnout-part-main-causes.aspx">Gallup research on nearly 7,500 full-time U.S. employees</a> helps explain why working conditions deserve attention. The factors most closely tied to burnout included unfair treatment, crushing workloads, unclear expectations, poor communication and support from managers, and unreasonable deadlines.</p>

<p>Work location may ease some pressures while introducing others. Working from home can remove a draining commute, for example, while making it harder to get timely help from colleagues. But neither arrangement automatically resolves an excessive workload or uncertainty about manager expectations. </p>

<p>Those problems require attention wherever employees work.</p>

<h2>Working apart can carry social costs</h2>

<p>The expression “work-life balance” implies that <a href="https://theconversation.com/when-workers-lives-outside-work-are-more-fulfilling-it-benefits-employers-too-260772">it’s healthy to engage</a> in social activity with friends and family outside work. </p>

<p>But as <a href="http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5386372">other research</a> of mine shows, more flexibility for office work doesn’t necessarily translate into more time with other people. Among younger workers in occupations that can readily be done remotely, I found that the share of leisure time spent alone rose from about 25% to 40% from 2017 to 2024. For workers who also spend their workday alone, that means fewer opportunities for socializing both on and off the job. </p>

<p>Time alone doesn’t have to lead to loneliness. But the finding raises a concern: Just because you gain more control over your schedule doesn’t mean that friends, family or colleagues will be available to share that time – or that you’ll make the effort to see them.</p>

<p>Related research suggests that these concerns about social connection deserve more attention. The expansion of remote work has been tied to increases in isolation and mental distress, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aec7671">according to new research</a> published by economists Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais. In a nonrandomized experiment covering almost 600,000 people, they compared changes in mental health before and after the pandemic in jobs that could and could not readily be done remotely, excluding 2020 and 2021. Remote workers living alone fared the worst.</p>

            </figcaption>

<h2>The next steps</h2>

<p>These findings raise a practical question for employers: How can time together at work become more useful?  </p>

<p>For employers considering a return to the office, a useful starting point is to first <a href="https://theconversation.com/remote-work-has-made-developing-relationships-with-colleagues-harder-heres-what-workers-and-bosses-need-now-194883">identify what employees gain</a> from being together and then organize office time around it. Teams that depend on frequent collaboration need overlapping schedules. Newer employees need access to colleagues who can teach them. Managers need to provide useful feedback and address workload issues wherever people work, and employees need to be responsive to managerial efforts to engage them.</p>

<p>Employee preferences and job requirements differ across organizations, so managers need to determine which arrangements suit their teams. But regular, useful feedback matters across on-site, hybrid and remote settings. That means discussing priorities, recognizing employees’ contributions and helping them work effectively with colleagues.</p>

<p>As Gallup workplace researcher Jim Harter <a href="https://www.gallup.com/workplace/700718/span-control-optimal-team-size-managers.aspx">has suggested</a>, this kind of feedback should become a weekly habit. </p>

<p>“These conversations don’t have to be long; 15 to 30 minutes, done consistently, is enough,” he wrote.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293319/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
