<title>AI can help with academic research but doesn’t always get it right – here are some tips to check the information you receive</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764338/original/file-20261006-50-zk2uv8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6240%2C4160&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">AI tools are not all the same – and should not be used interchangeably. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/powered-search-engine-interface-concept-with-royalty-free-image/2215176753?phrase=AI%20research&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Mininyx Doodle/iStock/Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Almost 25% of adults in the United States <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2026/06/17/americans-and-ai-2026-chatbots-smart-devices-and-views-on-impact/">are using artificial intelligence</a> chatbots on a daily basis, a 2026 Pew Research Center study found. </p>

<p>At the same time, another recent study found that 48% of the information that popular free chatbots <a href="https://www.statista.com/chart/35534/ai-chatbots-accuracy-rate-of-inaccurate-responses-2025/">gave in response to questions about the news contained errors</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=TQtfvy4AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">As librarians</a>, <a href="https://libraries.coastal.edu/prf.php?id=612ee872-7cdb-11ed-9922-0ad758b798c3">we know</a> that if students are using AI chatbots to help with their academic research, they shouldn’t assume that the information they’re given is accurate. </p>

<p>Not all AI is the same. Here are four steps we recommend to question information AI generates, including by checking the original source and considering issues that aren’t always easy to spot.</p>

<h2>1. Find the best fit</h2>

<p>First, we think it makes sense to spend time choosing the right AI tool for the task at hand. </p>

<p>AI tools – be it <a href="https://knowledge.exlibrisgroup.com/Primo/Product_Documentation/020Primo_VE/Primo_VE_(English)/015_Getting_Started_with_Primo_Research_Assistant">ExLibris’ Primo Research Assistant</a>, <a href="https://www.researchsolutions.com/scite">Research Solutions’ Scite</a>, <a href="https://start.chatcrafter.ai/chat/?">Anthropic’s Claude</a> or <a href="https://openai.com/">OpenAI’s ChatGPT</a> – are trained with various datasets and use different algorithms to generate results.<br>
They should not be used interchangeably. </p>

<p>Some tools might be better or worse at answering specific kinds of questions, and the <a href="https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/generative-ai-vs-predictive-ai-whats-the-difference">types of answers</a> they generate can vary. </p>

<p><a href="https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9260256-chatgpt-capabilities-overview">People might choose ChatGPT</a>, for example, at the beginning of their research process, because it can provide overviews and summaries to help with understanding concepts. </p>

<p>In subsequent stages, they might choose a tool such as <a href="https://knowledge.exlibrisgroup.com/Primo/Product_Documentation/020Primo_VE/Primo_VE_(English)/015_Getting_Started_with_Primo_Research_Assistant">Primo Research Assistant</a> or Scopus AI, which can help <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-peer-review-the-role-anonymous-experts-play-in-scrutinizing-research-before-it-gets-published-258255">find and examine peer-reviewed research</a> that has been vetted by academics. </p>

<p>Students conducting academic research could also see whether their library subscribes to an artificial intelligence tool <a href="https://researcher.elsevier.com/">like LeapSpace</a> <a href="https://consensus.app/?utm_source=google&amp;utm_medium=paid&amp;utm_campaign=search_branded&amp;utm_term=consensus&amp;gad_source=1&amp;gad_campaignid=20789663884&amp;gbraid=0AAAAAqgO5PIr_ok2BkYw_KEgaOnNZv0XI&amp;gclid=Cj0KCQjwuJLWBhD_ARIsAIBcRUzvWb-GIA_8gGu75DvOPsxar5Jepcc-zwN9zvqBGBMS6kzZCEwQWdEaAoB3EALw_wcB">or Concensus</a>, which draw their data from peer-reviewed, scholarly research. </p>

<p>Using these specific AI tools doesn’t eliminate the need to evaluate their answers, but it provides more certainty that the data has gone through a review process.  </p>

<p>Tools such as Anthropic’s Claude, meanwhile, may also draw from academic research, but to what extent is unclear. According to Anthropic, Claude states that it is trained on a proprietary mix of publicly available information from online sources, public and private datasets, user data and <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/transparency">synthetic data generated by other models</a>. </p>

<p>Finally, it can be helpful to <a href="https://guides.library.georgetown.edu/ai/tools">read librarians’ reviews</a> about AI tools to help select the best fit. People can also take a simple online test such as <a href="https://libraryguides.mcgill.ca/ai/literacy">ROBOT</a> to help them consider which tool to use. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764337/original/file-20261006-50-ux5xb5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A graphic image shows a person, seen from behind, standing in front of a series of brightly lit, purple, blue and pink screens with words on them." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764337/original/file-20261006-50-ux5xb5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764337/original/file-20261006-50-ux5xb5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=343&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764337/original/file-20261006-50-ux5xb5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=343&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764337/original/file-20261006-50-ux5xb5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=343&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764337/original/file-20261006-50-ux5xb5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=431&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764337/original/file-20261006-50-ux5xb5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=431&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764337/original/file-20261006-50-ux5xb5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=431&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Checking the primary sources on the information that AI tools generate is one of the important steps researchers can take to ensure it is accurate.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/data-personalisation-royalty-free-image/2208694533?phrase=AI%20research&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Andriy Onufriyenko/iStock/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>2. Ask more questions</h2>

<p>Second, asking follow-up questions is an important part of evaluating the answers AI tools generate. Even if the answer an AI tool gives sounds good, it is useful to take time to learn more about it.</p>

<p>Checking one’s own emotions is also important, because AI chatbots have been known to flatter users by giving answers based on the <a href="https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-algorithmic-mind/202508/ai-always-agrees-with-your-kid-thats-a-problem">user’s own biases</a>, or <a href="https://theconversation.com/ai-chatbots-can-prioritize-flattery-over-facts-and-that-carries-serious-risks-274298">what the user wants to hear</a>, rather than just facts.</p>

<p>Ask the AI to tell you where it got the information, how confident it is that the answer is correct and what might be missing. Ask the AI why it believes the answer is correct, or ask it to explain how it came up with an answer.</p>

<p>It’s helpful to also make sure your prompt is phrased in a neutral way. For example, asking “What does psychological research say about social media and anxiety?” rather than “Tell me why social media causes anxiety” may produce different responses. </p>

<h2>3. Check the source</h2>

<p>Third, it is useful to trace any claims the AI chatbot makes to their original sources. </p>

<p>Students may be familiar with using the <a href="https://hapgood.us/2019/06/19/sift-the-four-moves/">SIFT process</a> to evaluate websites. This process asks people to stop, investigate the source, find better coverage and trace claims to their original source. </p>

<p>Start by asking the chatbot to cite its sources, if it did not do that already. </p>

<p>Then, go to each source and read enough to figure out whether the AI is using the information in the right context. Also, look into who authored the source and whether they have expertise in the topic. If the AI won’t cite the sources it used, or if the sources it cites don’t include the information it said they did, pull out any claims it is making and do further research. </p>

<p>Can you find other, credible sources that back up what the AI is saying, using Google or a library database? Can you figure out where the AI may have gotten the information and whether that source is credible? </p>

<p>If this seems like a lot of work, you could always go directly to library databases instead of using AI tools. </p>

<h2>4. Not all issues are easy to spot</h2>

<p>Fourth, there are other, less visible issues that can play out when using AI tools. </p>

<p>For example, it might not always be easy to tell whether an AI tool is missing important perspectives or is giving biased information. </p>

<p>Remember that you, not the AI tool, are the researcher. It might be easy to rely on an AI tool to generate a summary of important sources, but deciding for yourself what sources to use helps you learn about a topic more deeply. </p>

<p>Research shows that most AI tools focus on sources such as websites, internet forums and other online content that is freely available and <a href="https://theconversation.com/ai-systems-are-built-on-english-but-not-the-kind-most-of-the-world-speaks-249710">written in English</a>. Consider what expert knowledge might be missing from AI datasets and seek out those viewpoints when needed. </p>

<p>Last, remember that you need to cite the AI tool you used if you are quoting or paraphrasing text generated by it in your work, just as you would cite any other source.  </p>

<p><a href="https://www.weforum.org/stories/all/beyond-access-why-ai-literacy-will-define-the-future/">Artificial intelligence is changing</a> fast. As librarians, we think it is important to continually evaluate whether the tools you are using are still working for you. </p>

<p>These tips are a good place to start to help sharpen your evaluation skills.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292865/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

For example, asking “What does psychological research say about social media and anxiety?” rather than “Tell me why social media causes anxiety” may produce different responses. 3
Check the source Third, it is useful to trace any claims the AI chatbot makes to their original sources
Students may be familiar with using the SIFT process to evaluate websites
This process asks people to stop, investigate the source, find better coverage and trace claims to their original source
Start by asking the chatbot to cite its sources, if it did not do that already
Then, go to each source and read enough to figure out whether the AI is using the information in the right context
Also, look into who authored the source and whether they have expertise in the topic
If the AI won’t cite the sources it used, or if the sources it cites don’t include the information it said they did, pull out any claims it is making and do further research

Can you find other, credible sources that back up what the AI is saying, using Google or a library database? Can you figure out where the AI may have gotten the information and whether that source is credible? If this seems like a lot of work, you could always go directly to library databases instead of using AI tools. 4
Not all issues are easy to spot Fourth, there are other, less visible issues that can play out when using AI tools
For example, it might not always be easy to tell whether an AI tool is missing important perspectives or is giving biased information
Remember that you, not the AI tool, are the researcher
It might be easy to rely on an AI tool to generate a summary of important sources, but deciding for yourself what sources to use helps you learn about a topic more deeply
Research shows that most AI tools focus on sources such as websites, internet forums and other online content that is freely available and written in English
Consider what expert knowledge might be missing from AI datasets and seek out those viewpoints when needed
Last, remember that you need to cite the AI tool you used if you are quoting or paraphrasing text generated by it in your work, just as you would cite any other source
As librarians, we think it is important to continually evaluate whether the tools you are using are still working for you

<title>Armed poll watchers: New Jersey’s 1981 racist voter intimidation campaign is a cautionary tale ahead of 2026 midterms</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762929/original/file-20260929-50-ml3i2d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=151%2C0%2C3864%2C2576&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Will voters in the upcoming Nov. 3 election face a voter intimidation campaign like New Jersey voters faced in 1981? </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/finger-with-i-tried-to-vote-sticker-in-front-of-royalty-free-image/1306559451?phrase=voter%20suppression&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Backyard Production, iStock/Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In the <a href="https://ugapress.org/book/9780820357744/voter-suppression-in-u-s-elections/">history of voter suppression</a> in the United States, including attempts to stop <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2020/04/11/opinion/sunday/republicans-voter-suppression.html">Black</a> and <a href="https://splinternews.com/the-forgotten-history-of-how-latinos-earned-the-right-t-1793862634">Latino people</a> from voting, Republican tactics in the 1981 New Jersey gubernatorial race stand out.</p>

<p>That November, voters in several cities saw posters at polling places printed in bright red letters: “WARNING. This area is being patrolled by <a href="https://www.wnyc.org/story/armed-men-once-patrolled-polls-will-they-reappear-november/">the National Ballot Security Task Force</a>.” </p>

<p>About 200 patrols were deployed statewide, many of them uniformed and carrying guns. </p>

<p>In Trenton, patrol members asked a Black voter for her registration card and turned her away when she didn’t produce it. Latino voters were prevented from voting in Vineland, while in Newark some voters were physically chased from the polls by patrolmen, one of whom warned a poll worker not to stay at her post after dark. Similar scenes played out in at least two other cities, Camden and Atlantic City.</p>

<p>Weeks later, after a recount, Republican <a href="https://njmonthly.com/articles/jersey-living/the-governor-at-80/">Thomas Kean</a> won election as governor by fewer than 1,800 votes. </p>

<p>Democrats, however, soon won a significant victory. With local civil rights activists, they discovered that the “ballot security” operation was a joint project of the state and national Republican committees. They filed suit in December 1981, <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/sites/default/files/legacy/Democracy/dnc.v.rnc/1981%20complaint.pdf">charging Republicans with “efforts to intimidate, threaten and coerce</a> duly qualified black and Hispanic voters.” </p>

<p>In November 1982, the case was settled when the <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/court-cases/dnc-v-rnc-consent-decree">Republican committees signed a federal consent decree</a> – a court order applicable to activities anywhere in the U.S. – agreeing not to use race in selecting targets for ballot security activities and to refrain from deploying armed poll watchers.</p>

<p>That decree <a href="https://www.npr.org/2018/01/09/576858203/decades-old-consent-decree-lifted-against-rncs-ballot-security-measures">expired in 2018</a> after Democrats failed to convince a judge to renew it.</p>

<p>The 1981 voter suppression efforts resonate today in the midst of the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/14/us/politics/supreme-court-trump-mail-in-ballots.html">Trump administration’s persistent efforts</a> to <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us-supreme-court-lifts-judicial-hurdle-trumps-mail-in-ballot-curbs-2026-08-24/">suppress the vote</a> and <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/trump-tries-to-undermine-trust-in-elections-but-documents-dont-support-his-claims">undermine trust in elections</a> nationwide.</p>

<p>In May 2026, a PBS reporter asked President Donald Trump whether he would send the National Guard or ICE to polling places in the midterm elections. </p>

<p>“<a href="https://x.com/ElizLanders/status/2054265101322993816?s=20">He did not rule it out</a>,” wrote reporter Liz Landers.</p>



<h2>The Republican ‘ballot security’ plan</h2>

<p>Considered an early referendum on Ronald Reagan’s presidency, New Jersey’s 1981 gubernatorial race featured Kean – with <a href="https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2008/06/02/the-dirty-trickster">Roger Stone</a> at the campaign’s helm – promising corporate tax cuts and relying heavily on Reagan’s endorsement.</p>

<p>State and national Republican party officials then devised a project they claimed would prevent Democratic cheating at the polls.</p>

<p>In the summer of 1981, the Republican National Committee sent an operative named John A. Kelly to New Jersey to run a ballot security effort. Kelly had previously served as one of the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1981/11/13/nyregion/kelly-reported-on-reagan-s-appointees.html">RNC’s liaisons to the Reagan White House</a>. </p>

<p>In August 1981, under the guise of the National Ballot Security Taskforce, Kelly sent about 200,000 letters marked “return to sender” to voters in heavily Black and Latino districts. Those whose letters were returned had their names added to a list of voters to be challenged at the polls on Election Day, a tactic known as <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/guide-voter-caging">voter caging</a>. </p>

<p>In the Newark area, Kelly produced a list of 20,000 voters whom he deemed potentially fraudulent. He then hired local operatives to organize patrols, ostensibly to keep such fraud at bay. To run the Newark operation, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1981/11/17/nyregion/imperiale-called-a-chief-in-gop-poll-security.html">he hired Anthony Imperiale</a>. </p>



<h2>Newark’s white vigilante</h2>

<p>Imperiale, in turn, hired off-duty police officers and employees of his private business, the Imperiale Security Police, to patrol voting sites in the city. </p>

<p>The gun-toting, barrel-chested former Marine had first adopted the security role during <a href="https://njmonthly.com/articles/historic-jersey/the-rebellion-in-newark/">Newark’s 1967 uprising</a> – five days of protests and a deadly occupation of the city by police and the National Guard following the police beating of a Black cab driver. During the uprising, Imperiale organized patrols of his predominantly white neighborhood to keep “<a href="https://nyti.ms/1Y8zykR">the riots</a>” out. </p>

<p>Soon, Imperiale became a hero of white backlash politics. His <a href="http://riseupnewark.com/Flyer-North-Ward-Citizens-Committee/">opposition to police reform</a> earned him widespread support from law enforcement. And his <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1972/12/05/archives/kawaida-towers-confrontation-in-the-north-ward-of-newark.html">fight against Black housing development</a> in Newark’s North Ward delighted many of his neighbors. By the end of the 1970s, Hollywood was <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1979/10/30/archives/notes-on-people-argentine-exile-fearing-reprisals-cancels.html">making a movie</a> based on his activities. </p>

<p>After serving as an independent in both houses of the state legislature, <a href="https://newjerseyglobe.com/legislature/14103/">Imperiale became a Republican in 1979</a>. Two years later, he campaigned with Kean. </p>

<p>Once in office, the new governor named Imperiale director of a new one-man state Office of Community Safety – an appointment often interpreted as reward for Imperiale’s leadership of the ballot efforts in Newark, but stymied when <a href="https://nyti.ms/29KrnJG">Democrats refused to fund the position</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762932/original/file-20260929-50-bnv55z.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A clipping from the New York Times showing a dark-haired man taking an oath." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762932/original/file-20260929-50-bnv55z.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762932/original/file-20260929-50-bnv55z.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=1173&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762932/original/file-20260929-50-bnv55z.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=1173&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762932/original/file-20260929-50-bnv55z.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=1173&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762932/original/file-20260929-50-bnv55z.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1474&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762932/original/file-20260929-50-bnv55z.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1474&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762932/original/file-20260929-50-bnv55z.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1474&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1982/01/20/issue.html">New York Times</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Outcome and legacy</h2>

<p>Despite Kean’s slim margin of victory, Democrats at the time were careful not to claim that Republican voter suppression efforts had decided the election. In 2016, the former Democratic candidate claimed <a href="https://www.wnyc.org/story/armed-men-once-patrolled-polls-will-they-reappear-november/">they did indeed make the difference</a>.</p>

<p>Rather, the state and national Democratic committees brought suit against the Republican National Committee to ensure it couldn’t again use such methods anywhere. For nearly 40 years – through <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/sites/default/files/legacy/Democracy/dnc.v.rnc/1987%20consent%20decree.pdf">amendments</a> and <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2009/12/03/us/politics/03voting.html">challenges</a> – the resulting consent decree <a href="https://talkingpointsmemo.com/edblog/this-should-keep-the-black-vote-down-considerably">helped curtail</a> <a href="https://www.democracynow.org/2008/9/18/lost_homes_lost_votes_are_republicans">voter suppression tactics</a>. </p>

<p>After the decree’s expiration in 2018, Republicans ramped up their <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2020/05/18/us/Voting-republicans-trump.html">recruitment of poll watchers</a> for the 2020 presidential election. After his loss in that election, Trump led a campaign aimed at <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-claims-2020-election-rigged-least-107-times-six-months-midterms-loom-2026-05-26/">discrediting the vote’s legitimacy, claiming fraud and irregularities</a> that he’s been <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/07/17/nx-s1-5896389/trump-revisits-debunked-theories-about-the-2020-election-in-primetime-speech">consistently unable to prove</a>. </p>

<p>Since winning in 2024, Trump has led a comprehensive effort to <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-supreme-court-blocked-trump-and-the-postal-service-from-restricting-mail-in-voting-for-the-midterms-291319">discredit and suppress mail voting</a>. And the Department of Justice, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon posted on X, has a “<a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/25/politics/trump-election-monitors-voting-machines-vis">plan to send 1,000 federal election monitors</a> to select locations around the country to observe the general election in November. This will be the largest monitoring effort in @theJusticeDept history!” </p>

<p>In addition to those efforts, CNN reports that “<a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/25/politics/trump-election-monitors-voting-machines-vis">the Republican National Committee is training</a> new ‘special monitors’ to scrutinize voting machines.”</p>

<p>This November, Republican tactics in 1981 are worth remembering. They demonstrate that the safeguarding of polling places from allegedly fraudulent voters and of public places from supposedly threatening people of color share not only a logic. </p>

<p>They also share a history.</p>

title: How October 7 changed everything
excerpt: Israelis visit the Nova music festival memorial site to mark the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023 attacks. | Saeed Qaq/Anadolu via Getty Images This sto
body: Israelis visit the Nova music festival memorial site to mark the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023 attacks. | Saeed Qaq/Anadolu via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Jewish communities in Israel and around the world are currently marking the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks that killed 1,200 people and triggered the war in Gaza
Memorials for the victims of the attacks have been held at homes , on highways , and at the site of the Nova music festival
In Tel Aviv, a massive art installation at the Trumpeldor beach commemorated both the victims and the 251 hostages taken by Hamas three years ago
Of those hostages, 166 have since returned alive, and the remains of the last deceased captive were released to Israel in January
But there’s no undoing the national trauma of the October 7 attacks — the deadliest massacre of Jewish people since the Holocaust — or the brutal retaliatory campaign that Israel launched afterward
Those events profoundly changed Israel, Gaza, the broader Middle East, and the United States, and they continue to shape global and domestic politics
So today, we’re taking a look at the very long shadow of the October 7 attacks and Israel’s response to them

Go a little deeper View Link Writing about the first anniversary of October 7 two years ago, Vox’s Zack Beauchamp warned that the “horrors” first triggered by the attacks would continue to unfold in tragic and unforeseeable ways . “Events that might seem contained to the Middle East have come to hurt people around the world,” he wrote, “in ways that we may not yet fully understand or even be capable of predicting.” That hurt has undeniably been most acute in the Gaza Strip, where three years of war have reduced entire cities to rubble
Israel’s military campaign has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — most of them civilians — since October 2023
Most of Gaza’s 2 million residents have also been displaced from their homes, crowded into makeshift shelters and refugee camps riddled with hunger and disease
But the consequences of October 7 extended beyond Gaza.  Settler violence against Palestinians intensified in the occupied West Bank
And the ensuing conflicts also weakened Iran and changed the balance of power across the Middle East
That’s because Iran had long relied on its allies, like Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon, to project power and deter attacks by its longtime rival, Israel

After October 7, however, Israel  significantly weakened both groups, leaving Iran vulnerable and setting the stage for the direct strikes on Iran that Israel and the US began last winter.  Both the war in Iran and the continued occupation of Gaza have badly hurt Israel’s international image
Across 36 countries  surveyed by Pew last spring, a median of 67 percent of adults viewed Israel negatively

That disapproval has translated into diplomatic shifts, as well: 155 countries — including longtime allies of Israel, such as the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia — now officially recognize Palestinian statehood, up from 136 before the war
That doesn’t change much on the ground , but it represents a real rebuke to Israel.  In the US, meanwhile, Israel has become a huge flashpoint in domestic politics
While more than half of Americans had a favorable view of the country before October 7, sentiment deteriorated sharply in 2025 and 2026, particularly on the left
The issue could help determine some key midterm races, like the Michigan Senate election, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has called for ending US military aid to Israel

That’s a policy nearly half of House Democrats and many potential presidential candidates have also endorsed .  Cutting off US aid to Israel isn’t likely to change the country’s stance toward Palestinians, however. (Israel is a wealthy country in its own right, and American aid represents just a small piece of its budget.) Instead, changing Israeli policy on Gaza and the West Bank would likely require far more aggressive pressure — pressure that, even in the current political environment, the US is unlikely to apply
A single day may have kicked off a cascade of hurt and horrors
But putting an end to them will take far more time
It can feel difficult (not to mention: naive, pointless, and exhausting) to maintain optimism in the face of current events

So Jamil Zaki, a psychology professor and the director of the Stanford Social Neuroscience Lab, suggests another tact: Do away with blind optimism and lean into hope — that belief that the future could turn out well, but requires real care and attention

Before you go… Did you know… that sea turtles regularly cry (okay: “shed tears”) to rid their bodies of excess salt? Scientists are studying sea turtle tears to learn more about animal navigation.  Today’s trivia: What’s the word for a baby eagle? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the final letter of the Greek alphabet
That would be omega, as in the Bible verse, Swiss watch brand, and nutritional supplement .

title: There’s a silver lining to your unhappiness

body: What can an economist teach us about misery?  I had that question in mind while reading the new book The Opposite of Happiness: How Bad Feelings Make and Break Us , by eminent researcher George Loewenstein

The field is not exactly known for its facility with human emotions, but Loewenstein is a co-founder of behavioral economics, the subdiscipline that studies the many ways that people depart from the ideal of the perfectly rational actor

He’s spent a career investigating how psychology and emotion shape our judgments, and his latest book offers a sweeping account of how suffering structures human life.  That might sound very bleak, like the opposite of a fun read
But the book itself isn’t distressing — it’s a bracing, useful, and even comforting lens on what it means to be alive

It emerged from a period of profound suffering in his own life, one where, he writes, he “thought about suicide constantly.” Writing it, he told me in a recent interview, was “kind of a silver lining for my own misery.”  In Loewenstein’s own words, The Opposite of Happiness is not a self-help book

Though he adamantly refuses to dispense life advice, I still think the book offers much that can help us live more wisely, a little less at war with our emotions.    “Misery is inescapable,” Loewenstein writes. “It’s not some malfunction or a bug in the system

It is the system.” Negative emotions are “more powerful, persistent, and pervasive than positive ones.” That is because, he argues, unpleasant feelings — hunger, pain, anger, loneliness — are how evolution motivated us to do the things we need to survive and pass on our genes

They still heavily shape our conscious experience, however mismatched they may feel to our modern circumstances.  Some version of that insight, that dissatisfaction is woven into the human condition, has been known to humans for eons, of course, captured in philosophical teachings like Buddhism’s Four Noble Truths

The father of economics himself observed that people work hard to earn riches, only to discover the result offers no lasting contentment. “It is this deception which rouses and keeps in continual motion the industry of mankind,” Adam Smith wrote in The Theory of Moral Sentiments. “It is this which first prompted them to cultivate the ground, to build houses, to found cities and commonwealths, and to invent and improve all the sciences and arts.”  Loewenstein puts this understanding into the language of modern psychology, speaking to a current of anxiety and unhappiness running through American life today

It also points to enduring questions about what the purpose of human progress and prosperity is, anyway.  Many of us could particularly benefit from the concept of negative “meta-emotions,” or the judgmental feelings we have about our negative feelings. “At the heart of so many of our miseries is not the fact that we feel bad, but the belief that we should feel otherwise,” he writes.  That line immediately rang true to me — merely acknowledging to myself that it’s not a big deal if I feel terrible from work stress, or my cat’s deteriorating health, or whatever else happens to be weighing on me, helps to lighten the load

What if we really tried to wryly embrace the reality that it’s extremely normal for life to suck sometimes? The reward might not be happiness, exactly (an elusive and poorly understood state anyway, Loewenstein points out), but a little less misery.   I recently spoke with Loewenstein about his book — he had a gentle, faintly melancholic air, and took a surprisingly generous interest in some of the choices I was weighing in my own life
Part of our conversation, condensed and edited for clarity, is below.  Americans seem pretty unhappy right now
There has been endless discourse about that
Do you think that your book adds something to that conversation? I do — I was just an expert on the Meta case that recently settled
I was an expert on the side that was against Meta
I think one of the causes of declining mental health is, in fact, social media
It really exacerbates the types of social comparisons that lead to envy and loss of self-esteem

I would like to think that I provide some new insights into how these modern technologies help to exacerbate the mental health crisis.  One analysis of that, based on what I’ve learned from your book, might be: We as humans are so guided by negative emotions, and often those emotions are relational in nature and have to do with how we compare to other people.  Social media is then quite naturally going to tap into and amplifying negative emotions that we’re easily manipulated by
One is there’s kind of a mismatch between the circumstances in which we evolved and the modern environment

And the other is that in the capitalist economy, there are, especially in the internet age, all these entities that are trying to exploit our evolutionary programming for their own good and not for our good.  The premise of the book, as you write, is that “misery is inescapable
It’s not some malfunction or a bug in the system
It is the system” — it’s like our default state
Can you unpack what that means?  I agree with everything you said until “default.” Different people have different set points, and there are some happy people around
My natural state is a little bit below zero

But there are very few people who don’t experience some form of misery frequently and intensely.  The evolutionary function of most negative emotions is pretty obvious, whereas the evolutionary function of happiness is sort of murky
And misery is so dominant that all it takes is a little bit of misery, a little bit of negative emotion, to wipe out any positive emotion
You go out to a really nice dinner at a fancy restaurant with your significant other, and you say something thoughtless and they get offended or they say something thoughtless and you get offended

All of a sudden you can’t even taste the food or appreciate the beautiful surroundings.  Paul Rozin at the University of Pennsylvania referred to this as the “roach effect”: If you drop a roach into a vat of fine French wine, you don’t want to drink the wine
But if you take a roach, you can add as much wine as you want to it and you’re not going to want to eat the roach
One of the strongest positive emotions is relief — which is interesting and not a coincidence, because it’s relief from negative emotions
It’s telling that maybe the strongest positive emotion involves the elimination of negative emotions
You can think of misery as a stick trying to get you to do things that evolution thought were good for you; the stick is very immediate, and you know exactly what it’s telling you
If you are hungry, it’s time to eat
If you’re in pain, you’re injured, you’ve got to do something about it
The carrot, which is positive emotions, you have to think ahead, Oh, if I did this, then I would experience this positive emotion
It requires a kind of second-order thinking, whereas misery is just immediate
Evolution figured out probably very rapidly, probably when we were single-cell protozoa or something, that sticks are a way better way to get an organism to do what it needs to do than carrots

How confident are you that the evidence base we have about the psychology of negative emotions generalizes to humanity as a whole and that it’s not culturally biased? “What I’d really like people to get out of the book is insight — into their own negative feelings, their own types of misery, and other people’s negative feelings.” Emotion researchers have looked across cultures, and they tend to observe the same basic emotions in a very, very wide range of cultures
What does vary across cultures is what induces the emotions
For example, shame — something that we would be unashamed of, somebody in a different country might be very ashamed of, and vice versa

title: Big AI has a problem on the right. It starts in Florida.
excerpt: Ron DeSantis speaks during a press conference on June 6, 2023 in Wildwood, Florida. | Paul Hennessy/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images If President Donald Trump ha
body: Ron DeSantis speaks during a press conference on June 6, 2023 in Wildwood, Florida. | Paul Hennessy/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images If President Donald Trump had his way, the Republican Party would be top-to-bottom the party of AI — or, in his preferred branding, “super intelligence.” But down in the very state where Trump has his “ winter White House ,” two Republicans have put forth a very different vision for the party’s future — and have been far more eager to take on the artificial intelligence industry
Ron DeSantis and his attorney general, James Uthmeier, have become vocal critics of the AI industry over the past year, warning of the technology’s dangers to children and to humanity as a whole
This sets them apart from Trump, who has championed the industry and downplayed its dangers
DeSantis tried to pass an “AI bill of rights” with child safety restrictions, but his effort was foiled by other Florida Republicans with close White House ties
Uthmeier has filed a wide-ranging lawsuit against OpenAI and the company’s CEO, Sam Altman
The two are betting that public backlash against AI will grow deeper, including among Republicans — and they’re hoping they’ll be able to steer the party in a post-Trump world
Ron DeSantis, who devoted much of his final year in office to a failed effort to pass an “AI bill of rights,” which would have imposed tougher restrictions regarding child safety and other topics

He’s warned that AI could “set off an age of darkness and deceit,” blasted “tech oligarchs” for putting people at risk, and called Anthropic “very creepy” for exploring whether AI could be conscious. “He clearly understands what the risks are, and I find he’s also very good at calling bullshit on disingenuous arguments from the Silicon Valley lobby,” Max Tegmark, an MIT physicist who co-founded the Future of Life Institute, an AI safety nonprofit, told me. (DeSantis hosted Tegmark at two events in Florida this year.) The other is DeSantis’s handpicked attorney general, James Uthmeier, a longtime close ally who is now trying to win the AG’s office in his own right — and who filed a high-profile lawsuit against OpenAI in June

Last week, Uthmeier asked the judge in the case to block OpenAI from developing new models unless they had “independent third-party guardrails and approval.” “The danger of these AI systems is real and growing,” Forrest Saunders, a spokesperson for Uthmeier, told me. “Florida and the nation have seen case after case of violence, child exploitation, and models that operate beyond their developer’s control.” He added that Uthmeier “welcomes innovation, but Floridians will not be the test subjects.” With AI cresting as a national anxiety — or a national opportunity, depending who you talk to — both major parties are still finding their footing on the issue

And though Trump is clearly trying to get Republicans in lockstep behind the industry, a very strong current is pulling the other way, responding to populist concerns and parents’ complaints to stake out a much more skeptical position. Florida has emerged as a bellwether for what Republican policies might look like if conservative America turns decisively against AI, especially as Trump’s political clock runs out

DeSantis and Uthmeier aren’t unique in the GOP for having concerns about AI — a handful of House members and senators want further action , and populist opposition to data centers has bubbled up in races around the country

But the two have gone furthest in taking on the industry directly — and they’ve done so even though it puts them on the wrong side of Trump.  In recent days, I spoke to several Florida political observers and advocates on the AI issue

Most believe that DeSantis and Uthmeier are affirmatively trying to stake out what the GOP’s position on AI should be in a post-Trump future, and to better align with an electorate that’s turning sharply against the industry, despite what the president may say.  “He’s trying to skate where the puck is going,” Jeff Brandes, a former Republican state senator, told me. (DeSantis’s office did not respond to a request for comment.) Beyond the quest for political advantage, the stakes are very real

Will there actually be a significant and influential force on the right that takes the concerns about advanced AI’s harms seriously — and is willing to act to try and rein them in, before they do great damage?  DeSantis and Uthmeier are hoping the answer is yes — and that they will be the ones leading that charge
Ron DeSantis’s quest for an AI bill of rights In this case, the politics and the personal are intertwined

DeSantis occupies a unique place within the party at this particular moment that’s given him an incentive to buck the national consensus on the right, especially when it comes to Trump, and explore an independent approach
In his first decade in politics, DeSantis had a charmed rise
In 2012, he embraced the Tea Party to win a seat in Congress; in 2017, he bear-hugged Trump to get his endorsement for governor

He then became a national conservative star for opposing pandemic-era public health restrictions and waging war on “wokeness,” winning his 2022 reelection in a nearly 20-point landslide. “He is always out front, even ahead of other Republicans, on issues that he makes more important,” Peter Schorsch, editor of Florida Politics, told me. “I would joke with people that I didn’t know how to spell ESG or DEI before he brought these to the forefront.” But what followed was a failed presidential primary campaign that put DeSantis on the wrong side of Trump and then sent him back to Florida with an uncertain political future.  Early last year, just weeks after a report that DeSantis’s wife Casey was considering running to succeed him as governor, Trump publicly urged Rep

Byron Donalds to enter the race, promising his “Complete and Total Endorsement.” Also early last year, DeSantis, who had long run roughshod over Republican legislators, was faced with a new thorn in his side: an ambitious new state house speaker, Daniel Perez, who was more interested in cultivating the Trump White House than the governor

Perez took a far more assertive stance in shaping legislation and rejecting some of the governor’s demands than his predecessors; he also publicly blessed an investigation into a charity tied to Casey DeSantis
A bitterly personal feud between Perez and DeSantis ensued

In the midst of all this, last summer, DeSantis got AI-pilled.  In July 2025, DeSantis announced that he was going to develop a state plan to deal with the rise of artificial intelligence. “We can’t just turn the reins over to a bunch of tech overlords,” he said . (DeSantis had long been a critic of major tech and social media companies on the grounds that they are too “woke” or politically hostile to conservatives and their ideas.) At another event that month, DeSantis said : “I think this is, like, the biggest issue that’s facing our society.” He mentioned AI’s potential impacts on the economy , on jobs, on students, and on the spread of “false narratives” as troubling to him. “I welcome technologies that will enhance the human experience
I do not welcome things that are going to supplant the human experience,” DeSantis said in September

His interest in state action put him on the opposite side of the Trump administration, which was advocating for a 10-year moratorium on state regulation of AI — arguing that forcing the industry to abide by a patchwork of state regulations would slow its growth. ( David Sacks , a key Trump adviser on AI, championed this argument .) Last December, at the Florida mega-retirement community the Villages, DeSantis rolled out his proposed “ AI bill of rights .” It did not focus on existential or civilizational risks, but instead more practical concerns around child safety
Megan Garcia, a Florida mother whose 14-year-old son died by suicide after conversing with a chatbot “companion,” appeared at the press conference

As introduced in the Florida state senate, the bill would have required that parents consent to minors speaking to companion chatbots and forced companies to disclose when users weren’t speaking to a human, among other provisions

But it was dead on arrival in the Florida House of Representatives — where Perez had aligned himself closely with the White House. “We do believe that the federal government should take care of AI, and whatever legislation or policy has to pass on a national level,” Perez said .  Brendan Steinhauser, who heads the AI safety advocacy group Alliance for Secure AI, told me that he saw Perez at a Mar-a-Lago fundraiser around this time, and asked him about safety risks. “He leaned to me and whispered, ‘We’re with you, but the president has made it clear not to move forward on this stuff,’” Steinhauser said. “So, the White House basically put the kibosh on that effort.”  DeSantis complained publicly that Perez was pursuing a “personal agenda” and thwarting badly needed legislation
It was to no avail — the bill didn’t move

But Perez did — Trump nominated him as ambassador to Brazil in June, and he was confirmed in August . (A request for comment from Perez, submitted to the State Department, received no response.) James Uthmeier’s lawsuit against OpenAI Though DeSantis hit a wall in the legislature, his attorney general was soon waging his own battle against OpenAI in court
The attorney general is an elected position in Florida, but when Marco Rubio vacated his Senate seat to become secretary of state, DeSantis filled the seat with the state AG, Ashley Moody

Then, to fill the newly vacant AG job, DeSantis chose one of his closest aides, who had served as his general counsel, chief of staff, presidential campaign manager, and chief of staff again — Uthmeier.  Uthmeier is a Florida native who had worked in Rubio’s Senate office; he graduated from Georgetown Law School in 2014

After that he joined the firm Jones Day and worked with Don McGahn ; when McGahn was named White House counsel in Trump’s first term, Uthmeier went with him to the new administration, ending up at the Commerce Department
Then, in 2019, he headed back to his home state to work for the new governor, DeSantis, and has been close by his side ever since

Now, though, DeSantis is term-limited, and Uthmeier is trying to get Florida voters to elect him for a full term as AG on his own. ( Trump’s allies had reportedly urged then-Speaker Perez to challenge Uthmeier in the GOP primary, hoping to supplant a DeSantis ally; Perez demurred, and Uthmeier won the nomination unopposed.) To make his mark, Uthmeier has filed several high-profile and politically charged lawsuits — for instance, he sued Starbucks over its corporate diversity politics (the company recently settled ), and Pfizer about the safety of its Covid-19 vaccine
He’s also subpoenaed the NFL over its “Rooney Rule,” which requires teams to interview minority candidates for top coaching and operations jobs
He’s also become the face of the administration’s challenge to the AI industry
In April, Uthmeier stood in front of a podium with an “Investigating OpenAI” sign, announcing he’d opened a criminal investigation into the company

The impetus was a shooting at Florida State University last year that killed two people and injured six others; the accused shooter had consulted ChatGPT about various topics related to his plans hours before the attack. “If ChatGPT were a person, it would be facing charges for murder,” Uthmeier said then. “This criminal investigation will determine whether OpenAI bears criminal responsibility for ChatGPT’s actions.” There have been no criminal charges yet

But in June, Uthmeier filed a wide-ranging civil lawsuit against OpenAI , alleging deceptive business practices, negligence, fraudulent misrepresentation, and other legal violations, because the company marketed ChatGPT as safe when they knew it could be quite dangerous

title: The cruelty of a beloved American pastime
excerpt: An angler reels in a ladyfish from the Atlantic Ocean at the Dania Beach pier in Florida. | Joe Raedle/Getty Images This story is part of a series supported by
body: An angler reels in a ladyfish from the Atlantic Ocean at the Dania Beach pier in Florida. | Joe Raedle/Getty Images This story is part of a series supported by Animal Charity Evaluators, which received a grant from EarthShare
When I was a kid, my family would occasionally go fishing on small row boats on the lakes of Montgomery County, Maryland
The point wasn’t to catch fish to eat — we always released them — but rather to spend time together in nature
And for a while, I looked back on those times fondly

But as I’ve learned more about fish and their apparent capacity to feel pain , I now wonder: Was I just stabbing a bunch of fish in the mouth and throwing them back in the water, injured and vulnerable? Ted Kerasote , a nature writer and lifelong hunter and angler, asked himself some version of this question decades ago after fighting to reel in a silver salmon in Alaska — the last he ever released

He still occasionally catches trout for dinner, but said that his decision to stop catch and release fishing that day in Alaska came down to looking at the situation critically: “Seeing this fish struggle for its life, for what end? I wasn’t going to eat it
Catch and release regulations were in place there
And so it was simply for my pleasure to fight this fish.” Each year, tens of millions of people take to America’s lakes, rivers, streams, and coastal waters to catch billions of fish
Many of these fish only exist because US governmental agencies put them there ; each year, over 1 billion fish are bred in hatcheries and stocked in water bodies primarily for anglers
And although firm estimates are hard to come by, it’s clear that the majority of fish caught are not kept for dinner, but tossed back in

Many fishing grounds actually require fish to be released (more on that later).  While anglers report being primarily motivated to get on the water to commune with nature, spend time with friends and family, and relax, the whole endeavor is anything but pleasant for the fishes themselves
After the steel hook pierces their oral tissue — and sometimes their eyes, gills, or esophagus — they’re often yanked around to the point of exhaustion before being reeled in
Then they’re exposed to air while the hook is removed from their body (and sometimes also for a photo opportunity ), before the angler puts them back into the water
There, the fish reenters an often-treacherous ecosystem while fatigued and injured
Sometimes, the hook can’t even be removed and likely remains in their mouths for hours or days
Estimates on what percent of released fish die vary widely
One 2005 literature review landed the average at 18 percent, while a 2026 review put it at 11 percent

But these are by no means definitive, as they each pooled together data from dozens of studies with different methodologies and time observed after catch and release, which limits our understanding of fishes’ survival from these encounters.  A different 2026 study , though also imperfect, took a more cleanly experimental approach
Researchers line-caught 489 Chinook salmon and then placed them in holding tanks for observation
Eight percent died within two hours of hooking, and about 25 percent died within 10 days
It’s reasonable to assume that the mortality rate would be higher if the fish were placed back into their local waters, with predators and other natural threats lurking
Even when fish are caught by scientists like in this case, the operation is by no means surgical

In the Chinook study, 90 percent of the fish experienced moderate to severe fin damage, around 45 percent had moderate to severe hook wounds, and 8 percent suffered severe eye damage. “No fish is better off because we’ve caught it,” Steven Cooke , a biologist and fisheries scientist at Carleton University in Canada — and an avid angler himself — told me. “It is impossible to catch a fish without causing, one, some level of injury, and two, physiological disturbance.”  In other words, recreational catch and release fishing injures billions of animals (a vast number of whom were bred for this fate) and condemns many of them to a premature death, and likely a more unpleasant one than if they had simply been killed humanely immediately after catch
Which means that what is often portrayed as a peaceful — even benevolent — pastime is, in another light, a more torturous activity

Especially if you think fish might experience pain.  What does a fish feel?  For much of recent history, it’s been thought that fish — far from us on the evolutionary tree, living in ecosystems largely foreign to us — don’t feel pain
But in the early 2000s, a group of scientists in the United Kingdom began to conduct experiments on fish that slowly undermined this belief
A seminal study, published in 2003, found that fish have nociceptors — sensory neurons that identify and respond to threatening stimuli, like predators or, well, metal hooks jabbed in their mouths

But it wasn’t necessarily evidence that fish feel pain in a similar sense to how we and other animals might; for that, a scientist would need to demonstrate that fish are not just reflexively reacting to noxious stimuli but also that their brains perceive it as pain
Since then, researchers have poked and prodded fish to see if something more is going on than mere threat avoidance

They have, for example, injected acid and bee venom into the lips of rainbow trout , whose respiration rates nearly doubled and who proceeded to rub their lips against rocks or the tank walls — seemingly in an attempt to soothe the injury.  In another experiment, scientists trained fish to feed in a certain part of their tank, and then subjected them to electric shocks in that area
The fish were less likely to seek out food as the shock intensity increased.  But Cooke, the angler and fisheries scientist, isn’t convinced

He wants fellow anglers to treat fish better insofar as he wants fish to reproduce, grow, and have a good life, but says he’s a “fish pain skeptic.”  “The evidence base around fish pain is meager and generally low quality, extremely biased, and unable to tell us whether or not fish have the capacity to feel pain or not,” Cooke told me. (Cooke, for his part, says he is biased too, and has received funding from pro-fishing interests.)  The core of the skeptics’ argument boils down to the idea that fishes’ brains don’t possess the necessary equipment to experience pain — namely, the neocortex, which plays a major role in our and other mammals’ processing of pain

Culum Brown , a professor and fish welfare researcher at Macquarie University in Australia, vehemently disagrees. “All [the information] we have to date suggests the behavioral, physiological, and psychological responses [in fish] mimic humans,” Brown told me. “Whatever way you look at it there are far more similarities than differences, which is not surprising given how important pain perception is from an evolutionary standpoint.” (Brown, I should note, has received some funding from animal welfare and ocean protection foundations.) We know that various species of fish can use tools , recognize themselves in a mirror , build artistic nests , form complex social relationships , distinguish between human faces , and maintain long-term memories , among other abilities

Is it such a stretch, then, to extend them the capacity for pain? Ultimately, as my colleague Marina Bolotnikova has written, the fish pain debate is partly a scientific one and partly a philosophical one. “The question remains unsettled because pain is a subjective feeling that science cannot prove definitively,” she wrote
One must be conscious to feel pain, and consciousness remains a mystery

With this uncertainty, we can continue to act as if they don’t feel pain, or we could give them the benefit of the doubt.  Georgia Mason , a behavioral biologist at the University of Guelph in Canada, is, like Cooke, not quite convinced fish feel pain

But she argues that we ought to take a precautionary approach and act as if fish can experience pain until proven otherwise.  With that in mind, should we be fishing for fun at all?  Reducing harm in sportfishing — and rethinking it altogether For his part, even as a fish pain skeptic and angler, Cooke is keen to reduce harm to fish
And the most important way to do that, he says, is to keep fish wet
He’s even on the board of a nonprofit called Keep Fish Wet .    Why? “Most fish do not do well when exposed to air,” Cooke said

Their gills collapse and/or stick together, making it hard for them to get the oxygen they need. “A fish should always be dripping wet,” and only out of the water for 10 seconds or less (the average time anglers kept fish in the air, in one study , was 29 seconds)

title: Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers
excerpt: Weight-loss drugs may slow biological aging
body: Weight-loss drugs may slow biological aging

Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their GLP-1 drugs aged roughly two to three years less biologically than those on a placebo, based on molecular "aging clocks" that track DNA changes and protein levels
The weight-loss medicines improve kidney function, lower blood pressure, and reduce overall risk of death
Big questions remain about healthy people

A $38 million federally funded study launching in Texas will test whether GLP-1 drugs slow aging in healthy adults over 60. " data-chronoton-post-id="1145836" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds

Drug giants Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their drugs age less quickly, according to readouts from molecular “aging clocks.” Such clocks assess a person’s biological age by looking at changes to DNA that accumulate with time, or, in newer versions, by tracking levels of key proteins

Both companies found that overweight or diabetic patients taking the drugs, called GLP-1s, had reduced biological age compared to those taking a placebo, although the difference varied widely, depending on which type of clock was used, and what organ was tested.  Overall, the difference was around “two to three years,” according to Nikolaj Roed, a global project leader at Novo, who says the company has been seeing “improved biological age in our patients across trials and across different tissues.”  The findings add to wide speculation among scientists that GLP-1 drugs, as they are known, are acting on basic causes of aging and might be a true longevity treatment. “Two years is a pretty strong effect, in my book,” says Steve Horvath, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, who’s credited with inventing aging clocks

Horvath says the emerging data could provide “evidence that these GLP-1 drugs are actually what is known as geroprotectors, medications that slow or possibly even reverse biologic aging.” The companies shared their findings over the weekend during Aging Research & Drug Discovery, a conference devoted to seeking scientific remedies for old age

While that quest has not yet produced any clear-cut success, some scientists now think Novo’s drug semaglutide (sold under the names Ozempic and Wegovy) is coming close. “In an unhealthy population, I do think it’s an anti-aging drug,” says Vadim Gladyshev, a Harvard biologist who assisted Novo with its molecular measurements. “But in a healthy population, no one knows.” The drugs cause weight loss by stimulating a receptor, GLP-1, that tells your brain you’re not hungry
Yet real-world studies have shown much wider benefit

The drugs improve kidney function, reduce blood pressure, and even sharply cut the overall chance of death. “If the question is,‘Can semaglutide reach several diseases relevant to health span and aging?’ we know we can say the answer is yes,” said Alejandro Aguayo-Orozco, a senior scientific director at Novo, the Danish drug giant, during the meeting

The next question to answer, he said, is whether such effects are accompanied by changes to molecular measures of biological aging: “When you intervene with semaglutide, does it actually move the clocks in any direction? And the answer is yes.”  The company found that, over time, the drugs cause a wide slowdown in aging clocks—as much as 4 years in the case of a clock that looks at heart proteins. “I think it’s pretty clear that the organ age is shifting,” said Aguayo-Orozco
The studies are also a huge boost for the science of aging clocks
Although these measures reflect a person’s age, it’s been uncertain if they are useful as true biomarkers

Now clock makers have evidence  that their readouts show a drop in age when people take drugs with broad, well-demonstrated benefits.   “The clock people have been pushing for a decade to get this kind of study done,” says Yuge Ji, a biologist who previously worked in the field and now runs a startup, Reflector Bio. “It’s huge for them.” As part of its study, Novo took blood draws from 10,052 people, half on the drug and half on a placebo

Their blood, collected at the start of the study as well as months later, was then measured with “proteomic clocks,” which use levels of key proteins to predict a person’s age and risk of dying .  Scientists at Eli Lilly performed similar research on their GLP-1 drug, tirzepatide, using so-called “epigenetic” clocks that assess age by counting accumulated changes to DNA

Lilly’s study was smaller, but also found that for the most part, molecular time moved more slowly for people on the drug.   “All the clocks are telling a consistent story that we’re seeing a reduction in age,” Kevin Duffin, vice president for aging research at Lilly, said during the conference. “It’s not like we’re going to reverse age by 30 years or something, but it’s a significant reduction.” The molecules have become the best selling drugs in the world,, with Lilly’s tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro for diabetes and Zepbound for obesity, topping the list with more than $36 billion in revenue to the company last year
Novo’s semaglutide, also sold under more than one name, was a close second

Alex Zhavoronkov, the founder of Insilico Medicine, and the organizer of the Boston meeting, says that extending lives by even one year across the world’s population would be equal to tens of millions of lifetimes.   Last month Zhavoronkov showed that one of his company’s drugs, for a lung disease, also reversed the signals from aging clocks
That drug is experimental, but Zhavoronkov has sought to promote the idea that humanity is entering a new era of longevity medicines

He also disclosed during the event that he has been “microdosing” the available weight-loss drugs, even though he is not overweight. “I am on tirzepatide and I am an equal-opportunity injector of semaglutide as well,” Zhavoronkov said

It was part of an effort to directly raise the question of whether the first mass-market anti-aging remedy is already here. “Do you think a reasonable person should start taking semaglutide?” he asked Aguayo-Orozco, the Novo scientist, in front of a crowded audience. “I am not a physician
I cannot answer that question,” Aguayo-Orozco replied
Several people cautioned that GLP-1 drugs do have side effects, including muscle loss

That is one reason they might not help most people, says Horvath, who says he isn’t ready to take the drugs himself, although he’s thought about it. “Clearly, the drugs have many benefits in obese people, but I did not yet see sufficient evidence that they will benefit skinny people,” he said. “I guess we will have to wait.” Answers could start to emerge in a year or two
This past January, a US agency, ARPA-H, put $38 million toward a study in Texas that will attempt to determine whether semaglutide has anti-aging effects in healthy people over 60
That research will look at changes in cognition, mobility, and acuity of the senses
That project also seeks to help define a regulatory pathway for anti-aging drugs and to “build a new therapeutic industry” around longevity.
